docs.text:
Global 
 What billionaires will do first if they’re hit with a new wealth tax
 Beckie Strum , Barrons 5 min read 3 Nov 2026, 04:45 PM IST 
 Summary
 Bankers for the rich with limited liquidity will help them decide to sell assets, use cash or borrow it. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Election Day is upon us, and so are wealth-related proposals on some state ballots.
 By several measures, the ultrawealthy—particularly those minted from the AI boom and yearslong bull-market run—have dwindling liquidity at the same time calls to tax the rich amplify. Inevitably, some will have to decide how to pony up more cash to the taxman if the handful of measures are successful.
 The states of concern on Tuesday are California, Colorado and Washington, where voters will decide whether millionaires and billionaires should pay more. Pass or fail, they are unlikely to be the last measures targeting the richest Americans amid growing income inequality.
 “Wealth tax ideas come in waves, and it’s experiencing some kind of wave right now,” said William McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation.
 All eyes are on a so-called billionaires tax on the ballot in California that would hit residents who have more than $1 billion in assets, excluding real estate, pensions and retirement accounts, with a one-time 5% levy. The funds would be used to fund healthcare in the state.
 A fierce fight over the measure has revealed the lengths to which the ultrarich are going to quash such taxes. Some of the biggest opponents don’t even live in California—or aren’t billionaires themselves, according to California Secretary of State campaign finance records.
 Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who moved his residency to Nevada last year, has spent $102 million battling the billionaires tax through his Building a Better California PAC. The organization has raised millions more from donors outside the state—with addresses in Florida, Oregon and New York. Texas billionaire investor James Coulter has given more than $2.5 million to Building a Better California, state records show.
 One of the main criticisms of California’s billionaires tax is that to pay for it, investors and business owners would have to sell assets, dilute their ownership stake and face the double-whammy of significant capital gains.
 There is truth to this. The rich have more wealth than ever by many measures—but not in cash.
 “Many of these people have built an enterprise, and they don’t have a lot of liquidity,” said Michael Cole, co-founder of R360, a peer network of centimillionaires and billionaires. “They don’t have $50 million or $100 million sitting around.”
 Cash allocations have shrunk in recent years. The Federal Reserve captured the trend when it published its mammoth survey on American finances in October. It found that the top 10% of earners have seen cash—in the form of savings and checking accounts—fall 14% between 2022 and 2025, a steeper decline than any other income bracket except for the lowest. It was the first decrease in transaction accounts recorded for the wealthiest cohort since the 2010 survey.
 Tiger 21, a peer network of nearly 2,000 ultrahigh-net-worth individuals, found in its most recent survey that members’ cash reserves are at their lowest level since the organization began tracking in 2007, as the rich shift their wealth into growth sectors.
 Tiger 21’s wealthy members hold a combined $265 billion in assets. Their cash allocation has hovered around 12% for nearly three decades until it began falling a few years ago, said Michael Sonnenfeldt, founder and chairman of Tiger 21. Cash is now down to 7%.
 “It’s an unmistakable, extraordinary trend,” Sonnenfeldt said. “The lowest it was before was in 2007, before the great financial crisis, when it dipped down to 8%, and you can draw any conclusion you want from that, but it does kind of jump out at you.”
 The trend was particularly stark in a Goldman Sachs retirement survey published in September. It found that more than one in three respondents with income above $500,000 live paycheck to paycheck. Nearly half of that high-earning cohort pay only the minimum or less on their credit card bill each month.
 So how is a cash-strapped billionaire (or millionaire in Colorado and Washington) going to pay higher taxes?
 It’s worth noting Prop 40 gives California billionaires the option of spreading payments in yearly installments.
 Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg went the “beg” route. In August, he told a special committee of Meta Platform’s board that he would have to move from California and away from the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park before Election Day. In response, the board created a new class of shares that Zuckerberg can sell to cover what could be a “multi-billion dollar tax payment,” according to regulatory filings last month.
 Zuckerberg aside, most people have only three ways to pay for an unexpected expense, said Katy Lingle, head of lending solutions at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. “You’re either going to sell assets, you’re going to use cash or you’re going to borrow money.”
 Borrowing is a clear winner. Right now, banks are more than eager to lend against greatly appreciated stock portfolios, offering credit lines with interest rates in the 5.5%—6% range. And the wealthy have shown a growing appetite for taking on debt.
 “If there’s a tax bill that you weren’t expecting to pay, that might be one of the things that you think about using a line of credit for,” Lingle said.
 Using a line of credit to pay a tax liability makes sense in a number of situations, said Houston-based Nickie Dupuis, head of tax services at asset management firm Cresset. For example, Dupuis worked with a Texas family that founded local banks that had grown substantially. “Selling any of that stock would essentially give a quarter of the proceeds to the IRS, which was not ideal for the fami

docs.title: SBI data breach: old guards, new threats
docs.text:
Opinion 
 SBI data breach: old guards, new threats
 Written By Vikram Koppikar 4 min read 3 Nov 2026, 09:38 PM IST 
 Summary
 How regulatory oversight and Data Legislation Interregnum impacted SBI’s data breach 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The State Bank of India (SBI), the country’s largest public lender, filed a regulatory disclosure on 21 October 2026, acknowledging a customer data exposure on the dark web, its primary audience was Dalal Street. SBI assured equity markets that the incident had ‘no material impact’ on core operations or financial stability. 
 The breach involving personal records, loan applications, and customer metadata signals possible institutional blind spots, Interestingly, the declaration was preceded by a warning from the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) regarding autonomous AI agents penetrating enterprise networks. In the following article, we explore how episode exposes not just institutional lapses within India’s banking sector, effects of delayed legislation, and the urgent necessity to retool defenses against agentic AI disruptions.
 Internal breakdowns at the lender 
 The operational failings at SBI span perimeter defenses, vendor governance, and customer transparency: 
 Detection Failures and Delayed Reaction: SBI learned of the breach on 16 October not internally, but from external notices issued by CERT-In, the Defence Cyber Agency, and a third-party threat intelligence vendor. Dark web claims had already circulated publicly on social media before the bank acknowledged the incident. 
 Third-Party Pipeline Insecurities: While SBI’s preliminary review identified 3,897 compromised records containing Personally Identifiable Information (PII), external threat actors claimed to hold over 375,000 entries and 2,722 loan documents. The presence of lead identifiers and loan application metadata strongly points to vulnerabilities in outsourced customer acquisition and direct selling agent (DSA) pipelines, where access controls and data-sanitization standards remain loosely monitored. 
 Absence of Customer Notification: While SBI complied with exchange listing requirements under Sebi (LODR) regulations, it issued no direct notices, consumer advisories, or helplines to affected account holders. In India’s banking environment, where social-engineering scams rely on accurate customer profiles, failing to alert individuals whose loan details, CIF numbers, and addresses were compromised leaves them directly exposed to targeted financial fraud. 
 Gaps in existing Indian legislation 
 The incident underscores significant structural flaws in India's data governance architecture:
 The Enforcement Void of the DPDP Act: India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act in August 2023. Under Section 8(6), data fiduciaries face statutory obligations and fines of up to ₹ 250 crore for failing to maintain reasonable security safeguards and to report breaches to affected individuals. However, the core enforcement provisions remain deferred under a staggered timeline until May 2027. Consequently, SBI operated in a legal interregnum, exempt from immediate civil financial penalties under the primary data statute. 
 Asymmetrical, Regulator-Centric Reporting: Existing mandates, such as CERT-In’s six-hour reporting directive and the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) cyber frameworks, require reporting to state bodies rather than to consumers. Furthermore, key measures such as the RBI’s March 2026 Advisory No. 3/2026, which outlines direct customer notification via SMS and email, remain non-binding guidance 
 Outdated Frameworks for Machine-Speed Threats: The Information Technology Act, 2000, and traditional regulatory frameworks presuppose human actors using predictable intrusion sequences. They lack specific statutory standards for automated tool misuse, API leakage, and autonomous reconnaissance. 
 Handling agentic AI disruptions 
 Previously, the CERT-In Advisory CIAD-2026-0049, warned that autonomous AI agents, both rogue research workloads and offensive open-source tools, have bypassed enterprise defences across Indian critical infrastructure . Because AI agents execute tasks across live networks at machine speed, traditional perimeter controls are obsolete. To insulate its digital ecosystem, India must implement a multipronged defence:
 Shifting from Perimeter to Micro-Identity and Least Privilege: Autonomous agents breach defences not through cryptographic zero-days, but by exploiting conventional lapses: hardcoded credentials, exposed API endpoints, and overly permissive cloud roles. Indian financial institutions must adopt continuous machine identity governance, enforce least-privilege role policies, and eliminate plaintext credentials across all code repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and middleware. 
 Real-Time Machine-Speed Anomaly Detection: Static, signature-based intrusion detection tools are inadequate against multi-agent swarms operating in parallel. Banks must deploy sub-second API monitoring capable of spotting non-human reconnaissance patterns, rapid data enumeration, and uncharacteristic bulk exfiltration before unauthorized sessions can mature. 
 Mandating Codified Breach Notifications: Regulatory authorities must turn voluntary best practices into binding requirements. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and RBI should expedite DPDP breach-reporting rules for critical infrastructure operators to enable redressal of impacted citizens without waiting for the 2027 enforcement horizon. 
 Detailed AI Legislation: Shortly after the incident, Union IT minster; hinted at a “white paper” aimed at regulating the harms that AI agents will cause. This remains a delayed response, as India requires immediate legislation to ensure secure AI deployment.

docs.title: Want to give back this Diwali? Here's how to find causes that matter
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Want to give back this Diwali? Here's how to find causes that matter
 Shefali Anand 7 min read 3 Nov 2026, 11:32 AM IST 
 Summary
 Diwali is a time for giving, but finding credible organisations can be daunting. Here's how to identify genuine causes, choose how to contribute and plan your donations. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 It's the season of giving, so why not consider supporting those less fortunate than you?
 Giving Diwali gifts to your house-help, driver and office staff is often routine. But for many people, the desire to give extends beyond festive gifts to supporting meaningful causes.
 “It just feels nice to share,” said Jyoti Khare-Pandey, a 51-year-old Mumbai resident who grew up watching her mother give to others and now tries to inculcate the same spirit in her daughters.
 If you decide to donate, however, knowing where to start can be daunting. More than 6 lakh non-profit organisations are registered on the government's Darpan portal, with lakhs more operating outside it. Some people hesitate to give because they are unsure whether an organisation will use their money as intended.
 “It's an overblown fear,” said Sumit Tayal, chief executive of Give, an online donation platform and repository of nonprofits. It was founded by the team that previously ran online donation aggregator GiveIndia.org, which shut down after covid. “There are thousands of highly credible non-profits doing amazing work in India,” he said.
 Mint spoke to experts on how to identify genuine causes and organisations that can help you make a difference.
 “The first thing you have to do is choose a cause,” said Shitij Malhotra, founder of toy company CocoMoco Kids, who used to run a non-profit until 2020.
 Once you have identified a cause you want to support, there are several ways to find the right organisation. One of the easiest is to look for a project close to home.
 Start nearby 
 Khare-Pandey wanted to do something for children, so she looked for organisations in her neighbourhood. She found Urban Community Development Centre in Bandra, which works with underprivileged children. Every year, on her children's birthdays, she takes them to the centre to make a donation. She also supports Dilkhush Special School in Juhu, which works with specially abled children.
 “You see the children happy, so you know the money is put to good cause,” said Khare-Pandey.
 She also supports healthcare causes, such as Shanti Avedna Sadan, a hospice in Bandra for terminally ill people. “You can see it right in front of you, how they help the people, how the place is maintained,” said Khare-Pandey.
 Another option is to look for causes in your hometown, said Malhotra. You can also ask friends and family for recommendations of organisations they have supported or seen doing good work.
 In addition, there are online directories of nonprofits, like Guidestar India and Give Discover , a brand of Give, which allow you to look up nonprofits by causes and geographies. These websites do some basic verification of the nonprofit, such as checking that it’s registered with the government. 
 They also offer more advanced certifications based on detailed verification and due diligence.
 Give, for instance, offers bronze, silver and gold certifications. It does not charge non-profits for these certifications but asks them to provide much more detailed information, said Tayal.
 Only certified non-profits can raise money on the Give.do donation platform, he said.
 Tayal said the platform also monitors how money is used after it is raised through fundraising campaigns on its website.
 Check before giving
 There are other crowdfunding websites, such as Milaap and Ketto, where individuals in need can raise money. These campaigns are typically for healthcare expenses and are based on specific needs.
 Such platforms carry out initial checks on people seeking to raise funds, including collecting medical reports of the person who needs treatment. In some cases, they also transfer the money directly to the hospital. However, monitoring how funds are used can be harder when donations go to individuals.
 Non-profit organisations, including small and mid-sized ones seeking corporate donations, would typically publish annual reports that provide an account of their work. Malhotra also places importance on the background and educational qualifications of an organisation's founders.
 Another channel for giving could be via your company, which may have verified nonprofits that it backs, and which saves you the hassle of research.
 Around festivals such as Diwali, some companies organise fundraisers with the help of Give.do. “We will do the monitoring to make sure that money that employees gave was used the right way,” said Tayal.
 Companies also offer payroll giving, which is a longer-term commitment, in which a certain percentage of the money is deducted directly from your salary. It’s painless, and “every month you get a report that your money was spent thus,” said Tayal.
 Give beyond cash 
 Money is not the only way to contribute. Goonj, a Delhi-based non-profit, accepts donations of old clothes and other materials, while DonateKart allows verified charities to run campaigns seeking essential products, including food and clothing. Non-profits may also directly ask for specific materials they need.
 Earlier this year, Khare-Pandey wanted to donate for Assam floods, and found a nonprofit through her friends. They asked for sanitary care products. “They told us, we’re going to shop, you pay directly to the company,” said Khare-Pandey.
 If you are unable to contribute financially, or want to do more alongside a donation, you can also volunteer your time.
 Many non-profits seek volunteers to support their projects. If you do not have a specific organisation in mind, platforms such as Bhumi list volunteering opportunities for youn

docs.title: Mouse movements & app switches: inside the software tracking IT employees’ activity

News 
 Mouse movements & app switches: inside the software tracking IT employees’ activity
 Jas Bardia 5 min read 3 Nov 2026, 01:09 PM IST 
 Summary
 ProHance CEO Ankur Dhingra addresses growing privacy alarms among India’s IT workers and explains why his tracking platform is essential for enterprise decisions. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Employees at India’s biggest IT firms fear they’re being monitored by software, but the chief executive of a company making such activity trackers is tackling two concerns at once: privacy fears among staff at India’s largest tech services firms, and the threat of those firms building the tools themselves. 
 Speaking to Mint last month, ProHance chief executive Ankur Dhingra said surveillance fears arise when the use of such software is "poorly communicated to employees." 
 “Think of it like a Fitbit, or think of it as an enabler that allows you to do your work from anywhere. So firstly, our software is fully in the end users’ control. The end user can switch it off, suspend it, change it, and not use it if they are doing something personal,” said Dhingra. 
 He added that the software drives better management decisions, noting that true productivity in large organizations can only be measured where the work actually happens. “So in our case, if you have these 500,000 users, unless you get a high quality measurement there, which is automated, which you can aggregate, which you can consume, which you can use, you will not be able to make effective decisions,” said Dhingra. 
 Explaining how ProHance measures productivity, Dhingra said the software tracks user activity across applications, such as time spent in team meetings versus other software. By aggregating these signals, the tool maps out work activity, application usage, and work sequences, which is then compared against output data. 
 His comments come after three of India's largest tech services firms—Tata Consultancy Services Ltd, Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, and Wipro Ltd—reportedly deployed software that tracks employee productivity.
 The rollout of these monitoring tools has sparked anxiety among IT professionals, who fear their daily work is being misjudged by automated metrics. "Tracking time we spend on our systems must not be related to output. We can work smarter and still do more on an application while spending less time than a colleague. This is concerning because we don't know if companies are tracking more than just time spent," said the employee of a company that has deployed such productivity tools. 
 Firms deploy productivity trackers to monitor time spent on work applications and log task outcomes. Mint previously reported that Cognizant and Wipro had expanded their use of employee tracking tools. Both companies have used ProHance in the past. 
 Mint first reported on 10 November 2025 that Cognizant was using ProHance to track mouse movements—something the IT major said was restricted to select business processes at the request of clients.
 Founded in 2009 by Kishore Reddy and Rajesh Sharma, Bengaluru-based ProHance employs around 300 people. In 2023, Mumbai-based private equity firm ChrysCapital announced its acquisition of a 75% stake in the company. 
 ProHance generated about $20 million in revenue last fiscal year, with three-fifths coming from clients based in the US. The company primarily serves IT, customer support, healthcare, and financial institutions, as well as back-end tech centres. 
 Competition risk 
 However, Dhingra faces a fundamental challenge: his clients can easily become his competitors. Phil Fersht, chief executive of HFS Research, said, “The biggest challenge for these technology vendors is that their customers are becoming much more sophisticated, while the technology they are selling risks becoming commoditized. Large IT services firms have extensive internal technology capabilities and can increasingly build their own monitoring and workforce intelligence solutions or integrate these capabilities into their existing enterprise platforms.” 
 Beyond the threat of clients building in-house tools, ProHance competes against global workforce tracking companies such as Sapience Analytics, ActivTrak, Time Doctor, and Hubstaff. 
 For now, though, Dhingra said he isn’t worried about competition from clients or rivals. “The special moat is the quality of the data collector we build, the fact that it can work across multiple operating systems, in complex environments where employees spend half their in VDI (virtual desktop infrastructure) and half outside it, and at the economics we can deliver,” said Dhingra. 
 He argued that IT firms are better off focusing their engineering talent on solving harder, more complex problems rather than attempting to replicate ProHance's software at scale, adding that most companies lack the deep technical expertise his team possesses. 
 He said the company tabulates best practices and has also launched a product to help clients monitor AI spending and utilisation. The company's software also alerts clients to job openings and helps employees evaluate the effectiveness of AI agents and related features. Dhingra said ProHance charges on a monthly per-user model, and the software cannot be customised.
 At least one industry expert noted that AI has increased the importance of productivity tracking. "Productivity is becoming an important factor on multiple fronts—internally to measure how AI is helping employees, and for contracts, where it serves as a critical metric that must be measured meticulously to ensure transparency for clients," said Namratha Dharshan, chief business leader for India Research at ISG.

 Jas Bardia is a Bengaluru-based business journalist covering India’s information technology (IT) services sector and Global Capability Ce

docs.title: AI is disrupting the art of campaigning
docs.text:
Global 
 AI is disrupting the art of campaigning
 The Economist 3 min read 3 Nov 2026, 04:48 PM IST 
 Summary
 Candidates are using the technology to crunch data—and carry out dirty tricks 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 IN ONE ADVERT James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, is depicted wearing a dress and singing about transgender children to a tune from “The Sound of Music”. In another Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, appears to be playing a board game and laughing at cards that read “Death to America” and “Celebrate 9/11”. These are just two of at least 220 campaign ads using AI-generated content this election cycle, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising. More than $137m has been spent airing such ads.
 Beneath the surface, though, artificial intelligence is disrupting the art of campaigning in more subtle ways. Candidates are using the technology to help them canvas more effectively, sift through voter data and craft custom messages. A recent survey by the American Association of Political Consultants (AAPC), a trade body, found that 83% of campaign strategists and political consultants regularly use AI for their work. The most boosterish insist the technology provides a decisive advantage for campaigns. Others fret that what few ethical restraints remain are being shoved aside.
 AI is changing how campaigns communicate with voters. Mr El-Sayed shelled out $170,000 to Daisychain, a company which offers an AI-powered platform that engages in personalised conversations with voters over text messages. Out on the trail, the progressive group Swing Left is taking a different approach, supercharging old-fashioned door-knocking with AI. Its volunteers record voice memos summarising conversations with voters. AI software then analyses hundreds of these recordings to help campaigns tailor their messages. “AI gives us a much better ability to understand the idiosyncrasies of a voter,” says Yasmin Radjy, Swing Left’s executive director.
 The technology is a boon for smaller campaigns on tight budgets. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful Democratic House candidate in California, had three staffers use AI to code replacements for virtually all the campaign’s paid software, from voter-outreach apps to website-design tools. Such efficiencies allow campaigns to focus on what matters most, argues Eric Wilson of the Centre for Campaign Innovation, which encourages conservative campaigns to experiment with new technology. “The core of what a campaign is about, which is connecting with voters, is still a people business,” he says. “The AI lets us do more of that than the boring, busy work.”
 All this is happening as AI increasingly shapes how voters learn about candidates. The AAPC found that at least 38% of voters had received election information from an AI search summary. So candidates are rushing to influence what chatbots say about them—a tactic dubbed “sloptimisation”. Campaign websites, for example, are increasingly designed to be scrapable by AI agents. Even adding information to a candidate’s profile on Ballotpedia, a sort of Wikipedia for election wonks, can affect the output of AI chatbots. But voters beware: a study published by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a think-tank in London, found that leading chatbots gave wrong, incomplete or outdated answers to over a quarter of basic questions about the midterms.
 That has heightened fears the election will be marred by misinformation. VisionHeight, a cyber-security firm, recently uncovered dozens of apparently AI-generated websites masquerading as local newspapers, designed to trick chatbots into pumping out favourable coverage of certain congressional candidates. Even more brazen are the deepfakes. A Russian disinformation network, for example, is thought to be behind a series of videos in which a supposed former student falsely accuses Mr Talarico of sex crimes. Elsewhere, attack ads depict Democratic candidates saying things they never said, sometimes without clear disclaimers that they are AI-generated.
 Of the $137m spent on AI ads, 88% has come from Republican campaigns and aligned groups. Concerns about such spots are overblown, says Mr Wilson, likening them to political parody. Voters may disagree. Any complaints they have may soon be fielded by artificial intelligence.
 Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

docs.title: India's new AI-training framework is a repeat of old mistakes
docs.text:
Opinion 
 India's new AI-training framework is a repeat of old mistakes
 Rahul Matthan 5 min read 3 Nov 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 The new 'Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training' framework released by the government does little to empower data principals while allowing those holding that data to gain. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Last week, the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) released a new framework aimed at breaking the “data deadlock” and democratizing data access to build artificial intelligence (AI) models. This new “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training” framework purports to enable responsible data sharing while ensuring privacy, transparency and trust . 
 I am not convinced it will achieve its aims. Not only is this not a novel architecture, it seems to subvert much of what India’s DEPA was designed to achieve. Decisions around what can be done with personal data, which under DEPA were placed in the hands of the data principal, will now be taken by the institutions that hold that data as fiduciaries—quite literally stripping away DEPA’s primary contribution to India’s data governance discourse. 
 Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) confers on individuals a right to data portability—to request that their personal data be transferred either to them or to another service provider. 
 Instead of prescribing how this should be implemented, GDPR left it to businesses to work it out for themselves. India, on the other hand, built DEPA, a data portability framework that gives individuals granular control over who their personal data is shared with and for what purpose. 
 As a result, it empowers them with the tools they need to realize the value of their digital exhaust. And when we implemented the Account Aggregator framework in the financial sector, we proved that micro-portability could work at scale. 
 If there was one mistake we made, it was calling DEPA a “consent management framework” instead of a portability solution. As a result, the term “consent managers” is now part of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, even though that term has a very different meaning in the data protection context. 
 This is why so many products marketed as consent management solutions bear no resemblance to how the term is used in the DEPA architecture. 
 But having made that one mistake, we seem determined to make things worse. 
 The DEPA for AI Training Handbook starts with the premise that individual consent is impractical at scale. On that basis, it takes the power to determine what is done with personal data away from the data principal and vests it in the hands of training data providers (hospitals, banks and the like), who will now be responsible for sourcing, curating and preparing the datasets for AI training. 
 I have long argued that consent is broken, and even that using clean rooms would strengthen DEPA. But DEPA is the one place where consent works, and when I suggested we use clean rooms, it was to enforce the consent provided, not to replace it. 
 The handbook also conveniently overlooks all that happens downstream of AI training. Since AI models are, in effect, massive data compression systems, they only need to be trained once on a given dataset to extract all the value they can from it. 
 The handbook does nothing to ensure that the data principals stand to benefit from the AI models they helped create—other than suggesting that training data providers could receive priority access to the resulting models and promising to “explore” royalties for them. 
 In other words, direct benefits will accrue only to model developers and the institutions that hold personal data, not to those whose data was actually used. It is hard to see how this framework can claim to treat the rights of data principals as “the bedrock upon which the entire architecture is built.” 
 But perhaps most disappointing of all is the claim that this is a uniquely Indian innovation—what the principal scientific advisor calls in his foreword, “an elegant, India-specific solution.” 
 Secure data environments are nothing new. In 2019, Finland’s law on Secondary Use of Health and Social Data required that individual-level data be analysed only in secure operating environments, and the UK’s 2022 Data Saves Lives strategy made secure data environments the default for accessing National Health Service data. 
 The handbook’s own evidence that the approach works is a 2022 project in which 71 institutions, led by Penn Medicine, trained a brain tumour model using federated learning within a “confidential clean room.” Calling this idea novel in the face of such a long history of use is disingenuous. 
 As accustomed as I am to techno-optimists masquerading as experts in legal design, the failings evident in this 40-page handbook exceeds anything I have seen before. It is a word salad of technological jargon and regulatory buzzwords that promises more than it can hope to deliver. 
 Electronics and information technology minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, in his foreword, assures us that it is “consent-based” and “user-controlled” even though the rest of the document says the contrary. 
 It was troubling when we took a novel and innovative data portability architecture and obfuscated the power of that innovation by mischaracterizing it as a consent management framework. But that seems trivial compared to what we are now doing—taking a tried-and-tested clean room system and calling it the next version of the DEPA framework. 
 Having not yet recovered from the damage caused by the first misapplied label, we seem bent on making the same mistake again. At this rate, the only thing that will be truly Indian about DEPA is the confusion we will create every time we do anything with it. 
 The author is a partner at Trilegal a

docs.title: What the midterms campaign tells us about where our politics are headed
docs.text:
Global 
 What the midterms campaign tells us about where our politics are headed
 Aaron Zitner , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 3 Nov 2026, 09:06 AM IST 
 Summary
 Party fracturing is creating a historic opportunity for a realignment where new candidates and policies break through. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Election Day caps a tumultuous campaign season during which anger at the failures of the political system exposed extraordinary divisions within each party.
 In Michigan last weekend, an astonishing Democratic rift emerged when the centrist Rep. Haley Stevens, who had narrowly lost the Senate primary, endorsed the Republican in the race and accused her party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, of infusing his progressive agenda with antisemitism.
 Republicans, in turn, have watched as President Trump elevated Ken Paxton, the indicted and impeached attorney general in Texas, for a Senate seat over a politically safer option, only to mock Paxton continuously on the trail as his campaign struggled.
 The seat is now in play, along with those in a handful of other states Trump won by double digits just two years ago, including Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Kansas. One reason is that Trump angered many of his own voters by imposing tariffs and waging war with Iran, leading to higher prices.
 The signs of the parties fracturing right before voters’ eyes came early, when Graham Platner, an obscure and unvetted oysterman from Maine, surged past the pick of party leaders with an angry, populist battle cry. “People know that the system is screwing them,” he said in a video launching his Senate bid. “They know it in their bones.”
 Less than a year later, his meteoric campaign imploded, and he was gone.
 The unruly nature of this year’s contests contains an appealing upside: the prospect that America’s unhappiness with the parties has grown so deep that it creates new possibilities for a political change, one that a swath of voters could find more satisfying.
 Many voters this year have been re-evaluating their allegiance to either political party, creating more fluidity in the electorate. Voters have elevated a new generation of political leaders who have the potential to reshape the parties. And voter dissatisfaction has produced surprising areas of agreement across party lines on how government can help people handle the cost of living.
 All three open the possibility that the parties have incentives to find new ways to become more responsive to voters. Tuesday’s elections will offer clues to just how much change can come from a new Congress and what likely will be the most wide-open presidential primary elections in years.
 “It does feel like we’re at an inflection point,” said Bill Haslam, a Republican former governor of Tennessee. “The question is, is something now going to come out of it?” The optimistic view of the public’s frustration, he said, is that “the ‘pox on both your houses,’ might lead to ‘let’s try something new.’”
 Voters reject parties
 Americans have been unhappy with their political leaders for years. In nine of the past 10 elections, voters have ejected one party or the other from its hold on the House, the Senate or the White House. The weight of history alone suggests that Republicans, as the party in power, have the tougher challenge this year.
 The GOP’s own campaign investments in recent weeks show them racing to preserve a House majority that is at high risk and that, more remotely, even its Senate majority could slip away.
 The dissatisfaction runs even deeper than in the past. Gallup last month found 15% of voters saying that most members of Congress deserve re-election, a record low in their polls dating to 1994.
 When Mark Putnam, a Democratic pollster, holds focus groups with voters, the anger reaches “an extremely poisonous level. One minute after they’ve introduced themselves, they start venting,” he said. “I’ve been doing this for 40 years, and I’ve never seen people as cynical and skeptical as they are now.”
 Increasingly, voters don’t see the parties as representing them. Gallup last year found a record-high 45% identifying as independents, and recent Wall Street Journal polling found a big jump in the share of voters who hold unfavorable views of both parties.
 While Trump remains by far the dominant force in the GOP, fewer Republicans now identify with Trump’s MAGA movement, Journal polling shows, and a range of GOP candidates in recent weeks have broken with the president by disagreeing with his tariffs and the war with Iran. Some party leaders are fretting that he took unnecessary risks this year in backing nominees such as Darline Graham, an inexperienced candidate who has put South Carolina in jeopardy of electing a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 28 years.
 Both parties have risked alienating voters with their tactics. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, ran an ad last month that was denounced as unseemly by the state’s governor and other GOP leaders for featuring his opponent’s estranged mother. In Alaska, the appearance of a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot for Senate raised accusations that the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, was trying to siphon votes from her main opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Her campaign has denied the claim.
 Rising stars
 In the wake of all this, the midterm results will show how elastic Americans are in their political affiliations—and what opportunity each party has to broaden its coalition. Meaningful shares of Latino voters, young voters, rural voters and some in the large bloc of working-class voters have told pollsters they may register their dissatisfaction on Tuesday by staying home or switching their support from one party to the other.
 A new cohort of young political leaders is now introducing itself to this more fluid voter pool. Sen. Jon

 This investment will enable Giva to strengthen its leadership team, build manufacturing capabilities and expand its offline presence.

 Jewellery startup Giva has raised over $100 million in a funding round led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management, alongside existing investors Epiq Capital and Edelweiss Discovery Fund.
 While the company has not disclosed its valuation, Ishendra Agarwal, founder and chief executive officer of Giva, said it was higher than the ₹ 4,800 crore valuation at which it raised its previous round. He said the current valuation was between ₹ 4,800 crore and the ₹ 6,000 crore valuation previously reported by Mint in August.
 The transaction also includes Giva’s seventh ESOP (employee stock ownership plan) buyback, reflecting the company’s commitment to recognising and rewarding employees, it said in a statement on Tuesday.
 The round comprises both primary and secondary capital, with existing investors India Quotient, Sixth Sense Ventures and some angel investors partially exiting. “The primary capital is for our own utilisation, while the secondary component is to give an exit to some of the older investors,” Agarwal said in an interview with Mint .
 Avendus Capital acted as the exclusive financial advisor to Giva and its shareholders.
 This deal underscores rising investor interest in India’s organised fine jewellery market. India’s jewellery market is estimated to grow at a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) to $124 billion by 2032.
 Giva plans to deploy the fresh capital across three key areas- offline expansion, manufacturing capacity and working capital. The company currently operates around 425 stores and expects to open about 160 stores this financial year, taking its footprint to over 1,000 stores over the next few years.
 “The capital will go towards offline expansion, manufacturing capabilities and working capital,” Agarwal said.
 The company plans to expand its manufacturing capabilities to improve product quality and speed up services such as lifetime plating and made-to-order jewellery. It currently has a manufacturing facility in Jaipur, while some production is outsourced.
 Giva is also looking to deepen its presence in tier II markets rather than prioritising international expansion in the near term. “Our first priority is to go deeper into tier II markets across the country,” Agarwal said.
 The company reported revenue of about ₹ 865 crore in FY26, compared with ₹ 518 crore in FY25 and is targeting growth at a similar pace in FY27. “We are on track to scale with similar growth numbers for FY27,” Agarwal said.
 The Bengaluru-based startup has grown at a 70% CAGR over the last three years, but is yet to turn profitable. Giva reported a single-digit negative Ebitda in FY26, an improvement from a negative Ebitda of about ₹ 17 crore in the year earlier. “The game is to become Ebitda positive next year,” Agarwal said.
 Giva has been building a "loyal customer base that keeps coming back for both self-purchase and gifting,” said Sridhar Sankararaman, managing director at Multiples Alternate Asset Management.
 “The timing is significant as everyday buying habits are shifting towards lightweight jewellery that can be worn daily,” he added.
 “What started as a digital-first silver jewellery business has evolved into a much larger proposition spanning silver, gold and lab-grown diamonds,” Agarwal said.
 The company's gold and lab-grown diamonds together contribute about 45% to its overall revenue. Its nine-carat gold jewellery offering, launched around four months ago, already accounts for about 25% of its gold sales, Agarwal said.
 Accessible options 
 Rising precious metal prices are also pushing consumers towards more accessible jewellery options, including lower-carat gold, silver and lightweight designs. “Consumers are moving towards more accessible alternatives of jewellery,” he said.
 In silver, Agarwal said demand was initially delayed this festive season, partly due to unseasonal rains that affected footfall in some markets during Karva Chauth. However, demand picked up over the weekend and eventually performed better than the company had forecast. He added that higher gold prices were also prompting some gold consumers to shift towards silver.
 Giva is also seeing a shift towards men's jewellery, lower-carat gold and lighter-weight pieces. “Men's jewellery is picking up very well,” Agarwal said, adding that consumers were increasingly looking for lighter designs as jewellery budgets had not risen at the same pace as metal prices.
 The company currently derives about 55% of its revenue from digital channels, including its website, app, e-commerce marketplaces and quick-commerce platforms, while offline stores contribute the remaining 45%, he said.
 On lab-grown diamonds, Agarwal said Giva was benefiting from its existing brand recognition and retail distribution network. He said prices in the segment had remained stable over the past one-and-a-half years, rising about 5%, contrary to concerns about a broader price decline.
 The company has adjusted pricing for larger-carat diamonds to remain competitive, while looking to expand its offering beyond smaller stones into diamonds of 0.5 carat, 0.6 carat and one carat.
 Founded in 2019 by Agarwal and Nikita Prasad, Giva previously raised ₹ 530 crore in a Series C funding round led by growth-stage investment firm Creaegis in June last year.  America’s Gulf allies prepare for new round of strikes on Iran—and the blowback
 Summer Said , Benoit Faucon , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 3 Nov 2026, 06:49 AM IST 
 Summary
 The risks are growing as diplomatic efforts remain stalled and Iran threatens unrestrained retaliation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—America’s Gulf allies are steeling themselves for a heavy U.S. bombardment of Iran that they expect to trigger a vicious cycle of retaliation against their own economic and civilian infrastructure as early as this week.
 Their concerns are heightened by a lack of progress in the various efforts to reach a negotiated end to the conflict while the U.S. and Iran are threatening especially ferocious fighting if the conflict resurges.
 President Trump has been leaning toward a large postelection attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, but hasn’t decided whether to go ahead, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Iranian officials said over the weekend their response to any attack would be unrestrained.
 “The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” Trump said Sunday at a rally in Iowa ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. “But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer.”
 Governments including Qatar and the United Arab Emirates were running security drills—including at airports—and attendees at a major energy conference in Abu Dhabi were cutting short their stays on advice from their governments. Schools in the capital of Saudi Arabia, which is also under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, will remain online this week. Dutch and Belgian embassies in the region warned Thursday that security conditions could deteriorate quickly in the region.
 Anwar Gargash, senior foreign-policy adviser to the U.A.E.’s president, said at a security conference over the weekend that the country hopes the diplomatic efforts will pan out, but is “braced for the worst.”
 Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said at the same conference that a new round of escalation would be more destructive and that efforts in the coming days or weeks would be critical to heading it off.
 The U.S. military has prepared options for attacks—restocking munitions in the region and beefing up defenses, including by moving troops out of vulnerable bases and sending another Patriot antimissile system to Israel.
 Trump has ramped up threats before, most recently in late July, only to back down in hopes of a negotiated deal.
 Tehran politely welcomed a letter sent in late October by Vice President JD Vance seeking to open talks with Iran’s top national security official, Mohsen Rezaei. But so far it hasn’t responded formally to Vance’s request to discuss Iran’s nuclear program and hasn’t agreed to a meeting, mediators between the two sides said.
 Talks in the main diplomatic channel, mediated by Qatar, are stuck on whether the U.S. or Iran should be the first to make concessions to move talks along, the mediators said.
 Gulf states are growing alarmed that they may face more destructive Iranian attacks than at the height of the war in March. Iran lacks the firepower to blunt U.S. and Israeli airstrikes and has adopted a strategy of quickly raising the stakes in any exchange by attacking its more vulnerable neighbors across the Persian Gulf.
 Iran has threatened publicly and in private diplomatic communications to attack a broad array of U.S. and Gulf targets in the region in response to any U.S. strike.
 “There is no world in which a short and sharp strike by the U.S. will be absorbed by Iran,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at U.S. think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “An intense infrastructure-based targeting campaign by Washington is likely to beget one by Tehran against U.S. partners.”
 Some Arab states have warned Iran they could retaliate individually or collectively if Tehran targets their infrastructure, the mediators said. The U.A.E. carried out strikes on Iran over the spring, but other Gulf states largely sat out the fighting.
 Gulf states are scrambling to come up with new formulas to break the diplomatic deadlock.
 Qatari mediators, who had previously proposed a seven-day period in which the U.S. and Iran would lift their restrictions on traffic in Hormuz to build confidence for further talks, traveled to Tehran on Friday with a revised plan that would cut the confidence-building period to two days, Iran says.
 Under one of the proposals floated by Qatar, the U.S. would loosen its naval blockade if Iran halted attacks on shipping in the strait for an agreed number of days, the mediators and an Iranian official said. Iran would then allow international nuclear inspectors back into the country and start a discussion on its stockpile of enriched uranium within a few days, they said. Once inspections are completed, the U.S. would lift some sanctions, they said.
 But Qatar has had difficulty nailing down an agreement. The U.S. is reluctant to lift its blockade before clear progress on nuclear issues, fearing Iran will buy time by rushing bottled-up oil shipments out of the Gulf, mediators said. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman said Monday there had been no discussion of nuclear issues.
 Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi returned to Tehran from Doha on Sunday after talks failed to yield enough progress to trigger a visit from U.S. negotiators, mediators said.
 Still, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran was willing to continue talks. “We are trying to solve the problem through dialogue. In this regard, the supreme leader of the revolution has also given the government certain powers,” he said without elaborating, state-run IRNA news agency reported Monday.

docs.title: Gold vs Silver ETFs before Diwali 2026: Which delivered better returns? What risks should investors check before buying?
docs.text:
Value Research data shows that silver ETFs delivered an average return of 25.04% over one year, compared with 15.79% for gold ETFs. Over three years, silver ETFs generated average returns of 35.96%, against 30.58% for gold ETFs. However, the recent performance paints a different picture. Over three months, gold ETFs declined 3.86%, while silver ETFs fell 17.04%. This highlights the sharper price fluctuations investors may have to contend with when investing in silver. The performance difference reflects the distinct demand drivers of the two precious metals. While silver has benefited from its industrial demand and investment interest, gold has traditionally attracted investors seeking a safe-haven asset. The three-month performance data also highlights the difference in their downside risks. Silver ETFs have corrected more sharply than gold ETFs, making it important for investors to consider their risk appetite rather than choosing a fund solely based on historical returns. Among individual schemes, Tata Silver ETF delivered the highest one-year return in the silver category at 20.51%, followed by SBI Silver ETF at 20.36%. In the gold category, Aditya Birla Sun Life Gold ETF topped the list with a one-year return of 12.93%, followed by Quantum Gold ETF at 12.89%. Gold and silver have different demand drivers, which explains why their prices do not always move in tandem. Gold derives much of its value from safe-haven demand, central bank purchases and investment demand. Silver, meanwhile, has a significant industrial component to its demand, with applications across sectors such as electronics, solar energy and manufacturing. Rahul Khetawat, senior vice-president and fund manager at 360 ONE Asset, said the two metals are fundamentally different commodities despite both belonging to the precious metals category. "Gold derives its value largely from safe-haven demand, central bank buying and investment demand. Silver, by contrast, is driven more by industrial consumption than by investment demand," he said. Khetawat said the global economy faces several headwinds, including trade tensions, the conflict in the Middle East, tight liquidity conditions and El Niño. In such an environment, gold tends to be better supported. "We believe that gold is better positioned than silver right now, and we remain more positive on gold," he added. Silver's higher historical returns come with a significant trade-off: greater volatility. Khetawat described silver as a "high-beta play on gold", pointing out that its industrial demand makes it vulnerable to deeper price corrections. He also noted that silver has historically been more volatile than gold, with its recent correction of almost 50% from its high reinforcing this risk. "Investors should size silver exposure prudently within their overall asset allocation, and keep a longer investment horizon," he said. Apart from the underlying metal's price movements, investors should examine five factors before selecting an ETF. Khetawat said both gold and silver ETFs are reasonably liquid and trade on Indian exchanges. However, investors should compare expense ratios, tracking errors and trading volumes across schemes and check the iNAV before placing orders. Investors should avoid choosing between the two metals solely on the basis of recent returns. Gold may be more suitable for investors seeking safe-haven exposure and relatively lower volatility within the precious metals category. Silver may appeal to those willing to accept sharper price fluctuations and take exposure to industrial demand. For investors looking to build exposure to either metal, Khetawat recommends considering a systematic investment plan ( SIP ) rather than attempting to predict short-term price movements. "Short-term price movements are difficult to predict, so investors should avoid trying to time the market and instead build exposure steadily over time, aligned with their asset allocation and investment horizon," he said. Ultimately, the choice between gold and silver ETFs should depend on an investor's risk appetite, investment horizon and existing portfolio allocation, rather than past returns alone. docs.title: Dhanteras 2026: Buying gold and silver coins on Blinkit, Zepto or Instamart? 5 things to check before placing an order
docs.text:
However, the convenience of doorstep delivery should not come at the cost of checking the authenticity and quality of the purchase. Consumers need to verify the seller, purity, weight, certification and final price before paying for a gold or silver coin online. Here is how to buy precious-metal coins through quick-commerce platforms and what to check before placing an order this Dhanteras . The process is similar across quick-commerce platforms. Open Blinkit, Zepto or Swiggy Instamart and enter keywords such as 'gold coin' or 'silver coin' in the search bar. Check the products available at your delivery location, as availability and denominations may differ by pin code. Select the coin after checking its brand, weight, purity and product description. Compare the prices of different denominations and check whether the listing specifies the manufacturer or seller. Before proceeding to checkout, review the final payable amount, including applicable taxes and delivery charges. Once the order is placed, retain the confirmation and invoice. At delivery, check the packaging and compare the product details with the original listing. Do not assume that a product is genuine merely because it appears on a recognised quick-commerce platform. The manufacturer and product documentation matter just as much. Gold coins are not covered by the same mandatory hallmarking requirements as gold jewellery. However, gold coins and bullion of 995 and 999 fineness can be hallmarked by BIS-approved refineries and mints under a voluntary certification scheme. Buyers should check whether the product is 24-karat gold and whether its purity is specified as 999 or 995 fineness. They should also look for the manufacturer's certificate or other documentation confirming the coin's purity. For silver coins, check the declared fineness, such as 999, and the manufacturer's certification. Do not assume that every precious-metal coin will carry a jewellery-style HUID number. A coin's weight directly determines how much gold or silver the buyer receives. Check whether the listing specifies 0.5 gram, 1 gram, 2 grams, 5 grams or another denomination. Consumers should also distinguish between the net weight of the precious metal and the total packaged weight. At delivery, compare the product details with the order confirmation and retain the packaging until the purchase has been verified. Gold and silver coin prices can vary depending on the metal's prevailing market rate, weight, purity, manufacturing charges and design. Consumers should compare the final payable price across available products rather than choosing a coin solely because its advertised price appears lower. Check the applicable GST and any additional charges at checkout. The invoice should clearly mention the product description, seller, price and applicable taxes. BIS also specifies invoice-related disclosures for hallmarked precious-metal articles. Before ordering, check whether the platform permits returns or replacements for precious-metal coins and what conditions apply. Under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, e-commerce platforms cannot refuse refunds or returns where goods are defective, deficient, spurious or materially different from what was advertised. However, buyers should not assume that they can return a genuine coin simply because they change their minds. Platform-specific return conditions may apply. If the delivered product has a discrepancy in weight, purity or description, photograph the coin and packaging, preserve the invoice and raise a complaint with the platform immediately. Consumers should save the digital invoice, order confirmation and payment receipt. These documents establish the product purchased, its declared weight, seller and transaction value. They can also help resolve disputes if the delivered coin differs from the product description. Ultimately, buying gold and silver coins through quick-commerce apps can save consumers a trip to the jewellery store, but convenience should not replace due diligence. Checking the seller, purity, weight and documentation before ordering is essential when purchasing precious metals online. Global 
 Iran turns to guerrilla tactics in bid to reassert grip on Strait of Hormuz
 Summer Said , Benoit Faucon , Georgi Kantchev , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 4 Nov 2026, 06:58 AM IST 
 Summary
 Tehran is deploying everything from rocket-propelled grenades to limpet mines as it attempts to disrupt the restored flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—Iran is using everything in its arsenal to try to stop the flow of oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz, resorting to guerrilla tactics to shore up the regime’s fast-eroding position in the conflict and pile pressure on the Trump administration in deadlocked negotiations.
 Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships over recent weeks, part of an asymmetric campaign targeting vessels that shuttle oil out of the Persian Gulf to waiting tankers, according to regional officials, security firms and analysts.
 The U.S. military runs near-daily operations to help ships—and crude oil—get out of the strait while maintaining its blockade on Iran, an expensive effort that nevertheless recently returned flows to prewar levels.
 The Islamic Republic’s battle to block that escape route has become a shadow war inside the wider U.S.-Iran conflict, with a direct impact on global energy prices as American forces have struck back.
 A spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment.
 On Monday, the U.S. attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island as part of a series of unannounced small-scale strikes in the waterway aimed at halting Iranian attacks on American assets and passing ships, The Wall Street Journal reported.
 Benchmark Brent crude traded Tuesday around $102 a barrel, with the average gallon of gasoline costing about $4.15 as American voters cast ballots in the midterm elections. That is up from just over $70 a barrel before the war.
 “They can keep it violent, they can keep risks to shipping high, they can keep costs high, they can keep oil prices high,” said Gregory Brew, Eurasia Group’s senior Iran and energy analyst.
 The Trump administration insists that it has control of the strait, and the U.S. military in the region says the waterway is cleared of Iranian mines.
 After flying over the strait last week, Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, said the U.S. maintained its patrols through the narrow waterway, which before the conflict was the conduit for 20% of the world’s oil supplies. “I didn’t see the IRGC out there, at all,” Cooper said, using an acronym for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
 October marked the highest monthly number of attacks in the strait since the war began, with more than 35 incidents logged by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center, which is affiliated with the Royal Navy. At least five vessels have been struck so far in November, UKMTO said.
 The attacks are designed to disrupt individual oil shipments through the strait and to re-establish the climate of fear that gripped shippers at the start of the conflict when Iran began to fire into the waterway and paralyzed shipbound trade in the region. A deal reached between Iran and the U.S. in June reopened the strait briefly, though Trump reinstated the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports as the two countries accused each other of violating the accord.
 For weeks, the IRGC has claimed that mines laid by its forces in the strait have damaged commercial ships, according to Iranian state media. However, Gulf officials say those assertions are designed to sow panic among shippers and doubts about the Americans’ demining effort, with the ultimate aim of disrupting the flow of oil.
 Since late August, Iran has used underwater, bomb-carrying sea drones to attack several commercial vessels, the officials said. Authorities in Tehran haven’t acknowledged the specific nature of those attacks, likely as part of the effort to suggest mines still litter the strait.
 Iran has also resumed the use of limpet mines to disable vessels, a weapon it deployed in 2019, maritime experts say. On Friday, in the waters of the strait just north of Oman, a small boat approached the port side of a tanker, attaching two explosives to the side of the hull above the waterline. The subsequent blasts caused a fire in the engine room and disabled the ship temporarily, UKMTO said.
 The U.S. Navy said Iran used limpet mines against ships off the United Arab Emirates in 2019, as tensions rose over President Trump’s withdrawal from the nuclear deal with Tehran.
 The scope and location of Iran’s attacks has expanded as more oil has started leaving the strait, going beyond tankers to strike containerships, bulk carriers and gas carriers including those anchored outside the strait elsewhere in the Persian Gulf.
 And, instead of relying on vulnerable coastal radars, which have been repeatedly targeted by U.S. airstrikes, Iran now favors human spotters, said Brew, the analyst.
 Crew on small boats operating clandestinely among the fishing craft that crowd Hormuz can observe passing vessels and relay targeting information to missile and drone operators, a type of surveillance that is difficult for U.S. forces to detect and disrupt.
 An Arab official familiar with Iranian attacks said such vessels often loitered around areas where attacks on commercial vessels occurred. Iran has seen much of its navy sunk by the Americans during the war, likely making the use of civilian vessels more necessary.
 “Iran can inflict significant damage at little cost, while the ability to launch attacks from numerous coastal locations makes it harder and more time consuming for U.S. forces to detect and prevent them,” said Alessio Patalano, a maritime warfare expert at King’s College London.

docs.text:
Opinion 
 Retail stress is apparent on bank balance sheets—we must keep close watch
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 4 Nov 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 Rising retail credit for non-housing uses, especially consumption, is a cause for worry. Especially since rural households will see borrowing costs rise even as their incomes may fall due to this year's super El Niño. Policymakers need to stay alert. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Over the past decade, one area of visible improvement in the Indian economy has been the resolution of the ‘twin balance sheet’ problem, in which the corporate borrowers were weighed down by heavy debt and the banking industry was hamstrung by record volumes of unproductive loan assets. A new bankruptcy code, aggressive write-offs, and recapitalization of state-owned banks helped clean up the mess. 
 With commodity prices and inflation staying low for most of this period, interest rates were at subdued levels, and helped repair stressed corporate balance sheets. 
 A recent report from Dun and Bradstreet on zombie firms—or companies where operating profits are lower than interest expenses for three years in a row—found there had been a broad-based recovery in the 2015-25 period, with the distressed tail comprising only about 14% of the sample. 
 This is significant because, without the attendant financial stress, these companies will now have access to fresh capital and be able to increase capital expenditure. 
 The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) June 2026 Financial Stability Report said the banking sector’s gross non-performing assets (NPAs) declined to a “multi-decadal low level” of 1.8%. Early indications also look promising. RBI’s data till 15 October shows 18% growth in bank credit. 
 Even sectoral deployment data shows that credit to industry (large, medium and small) till 30 September grew 19.5%. At a granular level, though, there are some niggles: growth has been more pronounced in the micro, small and medium segments of industry, rather than large. 
 There are other data asymmetries. 
 The latest print of the Index of Industrial Production for September came in at 6.7%, the lowest in four months, with almost all sectors, especially manufacturing (which has the highest weightage), exhibiting a slowdown. 
 Normally, production peaks in September in anticipation of festive demand; credit offtake would seem to suggest a manufacturing resurgence but production data suggests otherwise. 
 Significantly, all things remaining the same, RBI’s financial stability report envisages a marginal deterioration in NPA figures next fiscal year.
 Beyond zombie firms, there is a risk lurking elsewhere: the retail segment. The same RBI report indicates that retail borrowing as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) has been rising every year and reached 45.5% of GDP by September 2025. 
 In non-housing loans , those for consumption accounted for almost 50% of the household borrowings. This has risk analysts anxious, even though overall household debt is still below that for many advanced and emerging economies. 
 Borrowing for current consumption indicates income stress in households and raises the risk profile of these loans. RBI, in anticipation perhaps, tightened non-banking financial company (NBFC) lending norms for consumer loans in August. 
 Two top Indian NBFCs—Bajaj Finance and Piramal Finance—have already signalled early stress signals emerging from their gold loan portfolios. 
 With a super El Niño wreaking havoc on crop output and raising water stress, rural incomes are likely to remain under pressure. The turn in the rate cycle means that borrowing costs will rise. 
 Rural households will face the double whammy of declining incomes and rising interest payments. Policymakers need to pay attention to the household sector stress.

 Prosus looks to strengthen India bets on platforms and marketplaces
 Sneha Shah , Mansi Verma 4 min read 3 Nov 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The technology-focused investment firm, which recently infused $100 million in Sachin Bansal’s fintech platform Navi, is looking to deepen its financial services thesis, Ashutosh Sharma, India head at Prosus, told Mint in an interview.

 Subscribe now 
 Amsterdam-based Prosus is looking to invest in companies with platform or marketplace-led business models as it seeks to deepen its presence in India's financial services sector and other consumer-facing businesses, a senior company executive said.
 The technology-focused investment firm, which recently infused $100 million in Sachin Bansal’s fintech platform Navi, is looking to deepen its financial services thesis, Ashutosh Sharma, India head at Prosus, told Mint in an interview.
 Last week, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) approved Prosus's $100 million (around ₹ 940 crore) investment in Navi for an 8.5% stake. The entirely primary investment, one of the first institutional capital infusions into the company, values Navi at more than ₹ 13,000 crore.
 Prosus counts companies such as PayU, Vastu Finance, Mintifi and GrowXCD, among others, as part of its financial services portfolio. However, consumer-facing fintech was a missing piece [until the Navi deal], said Sharma.
 “If you look at the gaps in our portfolio, most consumer categories are spoken for. In food, we have something; in quick commerce, we have something; in mobility, we now have Rapido; in travel, we have an OTA (online travel agency) through Ixigo; in e-commerce, we have Meesho; and in services, we have Urban Company. But one big gap was a consumer-facing fintech platform. PayU is in our portfolio, and we own all of PayU, but it is largely a B2B payments and B2B credit business. So, a B2C fintech platform was a missing piece in our portfolio,” Sharma said.
 Founded in 2018 by Flipkart co-founder Sachin Bansal, Navi offers UPI, credit, insurance and broking services through a single platform. For the financial year ended 31 March 2026, its operating revenue rose 16.2% year-on-year to ₹ 2,981.7 crore. The company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹ 466 crore in FY26, compared with ₹ 126.4 crore in FY25, according to Tracxn data.
 Navi Finserv, the group’s lending arm, had assets under management (AUM) of ₹ 13,138 crore in FY26, which have already risen to over ₹ 23,440 crore by the middle of this year.
 “The interesting thing is that it is not a monoline business. It is a multiline business. They (Navi) have a UPI business, credit, brokerage and insurance. In that sense, it is truly a platform,” Sharma said, adding that the company operates in a large market with significant platform potential.
 Platforms over single-product businesses
 Prosus prefers businesses that operate as platforms or marketplaces, rather than companies offering a single product or service.
 “We have a very big affinity for platforms and marketplaces. Swiggy is that, Meesho is that, Rapido is that, Urban Company is that, and Ixigo is that. These types of businesses, which are platforms or marketplaces, we understand and appreciate slightly more,” Sharma said.
 The investment philosophy is also reflected in Prosus’s portfolio construction. The firm, which has access to patient, long-term capital, has built concentrated positions in companies across sectors rather than spreading its investments thinly.
 Its investment in Rapido is one example. Prosus first invested $180 million in the mobility platform in April 2022, when it was valued at $1.1 billion. Swiggy has since fully exited its ₹ 2,400 crore stake in Rapido, selling shares to Prosus and WestBridge Capital. The transaction values Rapido at around $2.5-2.7 billion, delivering nearly 2.5 times returns on Prosus’s initial investment in just over three years.
 Long-term bets, IPO-ready firms
 Sharma said Prosus believes India’s economic growth offers a long runway for its portfolio companies, making it worthwhile to maintain sizeable positions even as some of them enter public markets.
 “If you look at GDP per capita growth or overall GDP growth in our country, despite all the headwinds around war,fuel prices and so on, I think we are growing at a very decent clip. If, for a moment, we assume that some of these global macroeconomic and geopolitical challenges don’t exist, I think we have the opportunity to grow at this pace for many years to come, probably decades," he said.
 “Therefore, in my view, across most of our companies, even if they are listed, it is quite early in their earnings journey. Having concentrated positions in these companies allows us to ride this growth wave that our country presents for a few years, if not a few decades, in a meaningful way.”
 Rapido, Vastu Finance, PayU and Navi are among the late-stage companies in Prosus’s India portfolio, several of which could potentially tap the public markets as they scale.
 “There is no pressure from us. But I think at least three or four companies are ready from that standpoint. When they decide to pull the trigger is something I don’t know,” Sharma said.

Are large-cap stocks reclaiming their strategic leadership? Analysts' view
 Foreign institutional investor (FII) selling has been a significant overhang for Indian equities during the recent market cycle. However, the pressure has also weighed on several large-caps.
 | Image: Bloomberg
 Puneet Wadhwa New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 04 2026 | 6:30 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 After leading the market rally for much of calendar year 2026, mid- and small-cap stocks are beginning to lose momentum, with large-cap equities emerging as the more resilient segment amid rising market uncertainties, suggests a November 2 note from Bajaj Broking.
 With fundamentals remaining relatively resilient, valuations becoming more attractive and liquidity advantages intact, large-cap stocks, the broking house believes, appear better positioned to deliver superior risk-adjusted returns over the next six to 18 months. ALSO READ: The tide is turning: Smallcap AI winners are now facing a valuation test 
 Strong domestic institutional flows, argues Payal V. Pandya, Vice President, Prive-Research at Bajaj Broking in the note, along with abundant liquidity and sustained risk appetite had supported mid- and small-cap stocks through much of the year. However, the trend began to change during the festive season around September 11, when benchmark large-cap stocks significantly outperformed their mid- and small-cap peers.
