 Between September 11 and November 2, 2026, the Nifty 50 declined just 0.5 per cent, compared with losses of 7 per cent in the Nifty Midcap 100 and 6.6 per cent in the Nifty Smallcap 100. The divergence, Pandya said, points to an emerging preference for quality, liquidity and greater earnings visibility as investors turn more cautious.
 “While mid- and small-cap stocks have driven market performance through much of the current cycle, the recent divergence suggests that investors are placing a greater premium on valuation discipline, earnings visibility and downside protection,” the note said.
 Adding: “The question is no longer whether large-caps can outperform in every market phase, but whether the balance of risk and reward is shifting in their favour.” ALSO READ: Gold ETF inflows slow to ₹3,300 crore in October as AMCs suspend FoFs 
 The shift comes at a time when several uncertainties continue to cloud the market outlook. These include the implications of the upcoming US mid-term elections, the trajectory of corporate earnings, geopolitical tensions and the broader outlook for global economic growth, the note said.
 Against this backdrop, Pandya believes, large-cap stocks could offer investors greater resilience over the next few quarters. While they may not deliver the sharpest gains during periods of abundant liquidity and aggressive risk-taking, their scale, stronger balance sheets and relatively predictable earnings make them attractive when market volatility rises, the note said. 
 That apart, valuations, Bajaj Broking believes, also appear increasingly reasonable relative to historical levels, strengthening the investment case for the segment.
 FII selling 
 Foreign institutional investor (FII) selling has been a significant overhang for Indian equities during the recent market cycle. However, the pressure has also weighed on several large-cap index heavyweights, including companies that have continued to report healthy operating performance.
 This could create an opportunity if global risk appetite improves, geopolitical uncertainties ease or India attracts incremental foreign allocations, Pandya said. ALSO READ: Nifty Smallcap looks stronger vs Midcap index, can hit new high: Analysts 
 Large-cap stocks, particularly Nifty 50 constituents, leading private-sector banks and major financial services companies, are likely to be among the first beneficiaries of a revival in foreign flows, according to the note. Their deeper liquidity, larger market capitalisation and ability to accommodate sizeable institutional investments give them an advantage over mid- and small-cap stocks.
 “The investment case for large caps, therefore, is increasingly centred on their ability to withstand market volatility rather than deliver spectacular near-term returns,” Pandya said.

The tide is turning: Smallcap AI winners are now facing a valuation test
 Seven of the 10 top-performing small-cap stocks are linked to the US data-centre boom, but a global tech sell-off and high valuations threaten the rally.
 premium 
 Small-cap stocks linked to the US data-centre and AI investment boom have delivered sharp gains, but a global technology sell-off and stretched valuations are raising questions about the sustainability of the rally.
 Kairavi Lukka Pravin Palande Mumbai 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 11:43 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Seven of the 10 best-performing smallcap stocks over the past year have one thing in common: Exposure to the US data centre boom. But as enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) investment shows signs of cooling on Wall Street, analysts are warning that the rally in their Indian counterparts may have left valuations looking increasingly stretched. 
 The assumption that US technology firms will continue spending on AI at an unabated pace is increasingly being challenged. Any pullback in capital expenditure could weigh on the share prices of Indian suppliers, even those whose order books are backed by genuine demand. 
 Smallcap investors have had plenty to cheer over the past year, despite an otherwise lacklustre market. But the gains have been far from broad-based: Only 97 stocks in the Nifty Smallcap 250 index have delivered positive returns over the period.
 Among the biggest winners, Sterlite Technologies (STL) ranks second, with its share price surging nearly 526 per cent. HFCL has gained 180 per cent, while Aditya Infotech, Sansera Engineering, Acutaas Chemicals, Welspun Corp and MTAR Technologies have risen between 116 per cent and 194 per cent.
 To varying degrees, these companies have benefited from heavy capital expenditure by US businesses building out AI infrastructure and data centre capacity.
 There are notable exceptions to the trend: Shares of Cupid, a condom maker, have climbed 587 per cent; drugmaker Rubicon Research and electric scooter manufacturer Ather Energy have also posted substantial gains.
 One fund manager summed up India’s position in the global AI race: The country may be on the wrong side of the AI trade, but on the right side of the AI capital expenditure trade. In other words, even if India is not yet a major contender in developing frontier AI models, its companies can benefit from the infrastructure spending of global technology groups, including investment in data centres within India.
 The order books of some companies illustrate the scale of the opportunity. STL’s order book has expanded 4.6-fold since March to about ₹35,274 crore, supported by $1.2 billion (approximately ₹11,400 crore) in deals with hyperscalers, or large cloud and technology companies operating extensive data centre networks.
 HFCL’s management has said that a large portion of its roughly ₹18,500 crore fibre and data centre order book also comes from hyperscalers.
 But exposure to a booming global investment cycle can become a vulnerability when sentiment turns. 
 The recent retreat in AI-linked stocks, however, suggests that investors are beginning to reassess the trade. Over the past month, six of the seven companies associated with data centres or allied AI businesses have declined -- with the exception of Acutaas, which has expanded into semiconductor manufacturing.
 A Business Standard analysis of the combined market capitalisation of MTAR Technologies, Sterlite Technologies and HFCL found a growing relationship between the three companies and the Nasdaq Composite.
 An assessment of daily returns suggests that until March, the stocks moved largely in tandem with Indian smallcaps. By the July-September quarter, however, MTAR and HFCL had become more closely linked to the previous night’s Nasdaq Composite’s performance. A 1 per cent move in the US technology index was followed by a roughly 1.2 per cent move in their shares the next morning on the NSE. Over the same period, their relationship with the domestic smallcap index weakened by a third or more.
 The shift was also evident in the stocks’ sensitivity to the American index movements, or beta (the price volatility of a stock or other asset relative to the market). Earlier in the year, their beta to the Nifty Smallcap 100 stood at about 1.35-1.38, while their beta to the Nasdaq was close to zero. By July-September, the relationship had reversed: The Nasdaq beta had risen to 1.03, while the smallcap beta had fallen to 0.62.
 The pressure on Indian stocks has coincided with a broader correction in US technology shares. Over the past month, Alphabet, Bloom Energy and Meta have fallen 17 per cent, 26 per cent and 15 per cent, respectively. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks US chipmakers, has declined 17 per cent, while the Nasdaq Composite is down 7.5 per cent.
 Analysts are consequently becoming more cautious about the growth prospects of these 10 smallcap companies. Institutional ownership patterns also point to a more selective approach: Mutual fund holdings have declined over the past year in HFCL, Sansera Engineering, Welspun Corp and Acutaas Chemicals.
 The trend is not uniform. Sterlite Technologies, Cupid, Aditya Infotech, MTAR Technologies and Ather Energy have recorded an increase in mutual fund ownership in the September 2026 quarter compared with a year earlier.
 Market participants caution that the recent gains should not be mistaken for a broad-based recovery in smallcaps, particularly as valuations across parts of the segment have become stretched.
 “While smallcaps have done well this year, largely on the back of their superior growth profile compared with other segments and the emergence of new businesses, we have seen some meaningful corrections over the last few weeks,” said Amit Khurana, group chief executive officer (CEO) and head of institutional equities at Dolat Capital.

docs.title: Dixon Tech: 3 Buy calls vs 1 Reduce — Can expansion drive a 64% stock rally?
docs.text: Dixon Technologies share price in in focus as the company is at an important point in its expansion. Its ambitions now extend well beyond assembling smartphones, with plans to build a larger presence in IT hardware, exports and electronic components. Higher input prices, the withdrawal of production incentives and the addition of lower-margin businesses are testing the company's profitability even as its revenue grows. This has created a divide among brokerages over the stock's near-term prospects and valuation. Emkay Global, Anand Rathi and Nomura remain positive, betting on new customer relationships, export opportunities and manufacturing expansion. Elara Securities has, however, turned cautious, arguing that the pace of earnings growth is slowing and margin pressures could persist. The brokerage sees exports, new customer additions and the expansion of the company's manufacturing capabilities as important growth drivers, although it has adjusted its earnings estimates to account for margin pressures. ALSO READ3 Smallcap Stocks Trading Near 52-week Lows “Exports to see growth ahead, largely driven by Motorola,” Emkay said. Emkay's analysis points to a gradual increase in export volumes, particularly through Motorola, as one of the factors supporting its mobile business outlook. The brokerage has also examined the contribution from existing and prospective customers, including the impact of volume changes at brands such as Transsion, Xiaomi and Samsung. ALSO READWhy Nomura signals earnings slowdown after $53 bn outflows shrink holdings to historic lows It expects smartphone volumes, excluding Vivo, to remain an important part of Dixon's business. The company is also preparing to scale up the Vivo joint venture, while a new domestic brand customer is expected to contribute additional volumes. Emkay sees the export opportunity as a further source of growth as manufacturing programmes ramp up. The brokerage has, however, factored in pressure on profitability. Its estimates reflect the absence of mobile PLI benefits in FY27 and the impact of lower-margin business segments. It expects EBITDA margins to improve over the forecast period as production scales up and localisation increases. IT hardware is another growth opportunity. Dixon is expanding its presence in laptops, tablets and related products, while also increasing its capabilities in components. Emkay believes these businesses can broaden the company's revenue base, although their contribution to margins will depend on scale and backward integration. Anand Rathi on Dixon Anand Rathi has retained its 'Buy' rating on Dixon with a target price of Rs 18,000, implying an upside of about 63.6%. The brokerage values the company at 45 times its estimated earnings for the first half of FY29 and sees strong medium-term growth potential from customer additions, exports and new manufacturing programmes. Anand Rathi highlighted that Dixon's Q2FY27 EBITDA was 12% above its estimate, supported by better-than-expected mobile volumes. The company continued to gain market share even as smartphone industry volumes declined during the quarter. Beyond mobile phones, Anand Rathi sees opportunities in IT hardware, telecom and networking. The Inventec and Gemtek joint ventures could give Dixon access to global IT hardware and data centre-related opportunities. Localisation of display and camera modules could also provide a route to better margins. Nomura on Dixon Nomura has retained its 'Buy' rating on Dixon but reduced its target price to Rs 15,664 from Rs 17,086. The revised target implies an upside of 42.4%. The brokerage continues to see opportunities in mobile manufacturing, exports and IT hardware, while acknowledging that cost pressures have affected its margin assumptions. “In smartphones, we believe Dixon has multiple catalysts from customer additions, exports (MPMS link) and Longcheer JV (603341 CH, Not rated; link) which should help drive growth despite weak domestic demand. Hence, we trim our FY27F volumes to 36mn (delay in Vivo JV) but maintain 54mn/60mn for FY28F Higher ASPs lead to an ~8% rise in revenues for FY28F/29F,” Nomura added. Nomura has lowered its FY27 volume estimate to 36 million units, factoring in the delay in the Vivo joint venture's ramp-up. It has retained its FY28 and FY29 volume estimates at 54 million and 60 million units, respectively. Nomura sees the Vivo joint venture, new Indian brand customers and exports as important drivers of the next phase of mobile manufacturing growth. It also expects the IT hardware business to expand through laptops, tablets and servers, with management indicating a potential revenue opportunity of Rs 15,000-20,000 crore over the next two years. Component manufacturing is another area of focus. Dixon is expanding camera module capacity and developing display module manufacturing through its joint venture with HKC. Nomura believes greater domestic value addition could support margin expansion over time. Elara on Dixon Elara Securities has taken the most cautious stance among the four brokerages. It has downgraded Dixon to 'Reduce' from 'Accumulate' and cut its target price to Rs 11,500 from Rs 14,980. The revised target implies an upside of about 4.5%. Elara's concern is that higher sales value does not necessarily indicate a corresponding improvement in underlying demand. It points to the sharp rise in memory module prices as a key reason for the increase in average selling prices, while the broader mobile industry has faced a decline in volumes, particularly in the entry- and mid-level segments. docs.title: ITC share price: Jefferies sees 32% upside ahead but Motilal Oswal stays cautious
docs.text: The ITC share price tarded in green up over 1% after the Q2 results. Its cigarette business is going through a difficult phase, but Jefferies believes the pressure could gradually ease. The global investment bank has retained its positive stance on the stock, even as it trims its earnings estimates. Motilal Oswal, meanwhile, is more cautious, pointing to the pressure on cigarette earnings and the time it could take for price increases to fully offset higher taxes. Jefferies sees encouraging signs across the company’s businesses and expects a gradual improvement in cigarette profitability over the coming years. The difference between the two brokerage house is reflected in their recommendations. Jefferies has maintained a 'Buy' rating with a target price of Rs 350, while Motilal Oswal has a 'Neutral' rating and a target price of Rs 285. Jefferies on ITC Jefferies has maintained a 'Buy' rating on ITC with a target price of Rs 350, implying an upside of 32%. The brokerage’s optimism rests on the possibility of a gradual recovery in cigarette volumes, alongside continued momentum in ITC’s other businesses. In its investment thesis, Jefferies said, “ITC is seeing good momentum across businesses. Sustained volume recovery in cigarettes due to share gains from illicit cigarettes is encouraging.” The potential recovery in cigarette volumes is important because the business remains the largest contributor to ITC’s valuation. Jefferies believes gains in market share from illicit cigarette operators could support volumes, while growth in FMCG offers another source of support. The brokerage has, however, factored in near-term weakness. It has trimmed its FY27-29 earnings estimates by 2-3%, while retaining its sum-of-the-parts-based target price. Motilal Oswal on ITC Motilal Oswal has maintained a 'Neutral' rating on ITC with a target price of Rs 285, implying an upside of 7%. The brokerage’s report, titled Cigarette EBIT pressure sustains; beat on FMCG performance, highlights the continuing weakness in cigarette earnings. It noted that the company has adopted a calibrated price-hike strategy after the sharp increase in taxes, rather than passing on the entire impact immediately. According to Motilal Oswal, the approach is intended to protect consumers from shifting from the legal to the illegal cigarette market. Price increases are still being implemented, but the cumulative hike has not yet reached the tax-neutral level. The brokerage also highlighted the stronger performance of FMCG, where sales grew 19% and EBIT increased 31%. Agriculture revenue rose 13%, while paper business sales increased 36%. Despite the improvement in these segments, Motilal Oswal remains cautious about the cigarette business and has retained its 'Neutral' stance. ITC: Cigarette earnings face near-term pressure ITC’s cigarette business remained under pressure in the September quarter. Jefferies estimated that cigarette volumes declined by around 8% year-on-year, while cigarette net revenue fell 21%. Segment EBIT declined 27%. Cigarette EBIT margin stood at 65.3%, down 560 basis points year-on-year, although it improved sequentially. Segment EBIT came in at Rs 38.1 billion, compared with Rs 52.4 billion in the corresponding quarter last year. Jefferies expects cigarette revenue to decline 7% in FY27, with volumes falling 6%. It forecasts cigarette EBIT to drop 21% during the year, followed by a recovery of 13% in FY28 and another 10% increase in FY29. In its base-case assumptions, the brokerage expects cigarette EBIT to remain broadly flat over FY26-29. Its positive view therefore rests on a gradual improvement rather than an immediate turnaround. ALSO READAshish Kacholia’s Rs 51 cr IPO stake, Sunil Singhania’s Rs 250 cr auto play: Latest moves Jefferies has also identified a sharp increase in taxation as a downside risk. On the other hand, a recovery in cigarette volumes as ITC regains share from illicit trade could provide an upside trigger. ITC: FMCG business provides a growth cushion While cigarettes remain under pressure, ITC’s FMCG business has delivered a stronger performance. Jefferies reported 17% growth in FMCG revenue, with several categories recording growth of more than 20%. Dairy and personal wash also posted growth in the high teens. The segment’s EBITDA margin improved by 50 basis points. Jefferies also highlighted the performance of ITC’s digital-first and organic portfolio, which grew 70%, taking its annualised revenue run rate above Rs 18 billion. The brokerage sees the FMCG business as an important part of ITC’s longer-term growth and valuation story. In its sum-of-the-parts valuation, FMCG accounts for 28% of the company’s value, while cigarettes account for 55%. Paperboards and agriculture add to the momentum ITC’s paperboards, paper and packaging business also reported growth. Revenue increased 36%, partly reflecting the acquisition of Century Pulp & Paper. On a like-for-like basis, revenue rose 10%. Jefferies noted that segment EBIT increased 48%, with margins improving by 70 basis points. ALSO READITC Q2 results: Net profit falls 20% to Rs 4,137 crore, revenue rises 44% The agriculture business recorded 12% revenue growth and 11% EBIT growth. However, the brokerage flagged geopolitical tensions, elevated crude and input costs, and inflationary pressures as risks to the operating environment. It also noted that uneven monsoons and El Niño could affect agricultural output and inflation. Overall, Jefferies believes ITC is seeing momentum across businesses, even though the cigarette segment is likely to take time to recover. docs.title: Affle India to GE Vernova T&D: Ambit Capital names 5 stocks with 22% to 49% upside
docs.text: Picking stocks is as much about understanding a company's next growth opportunity as it is about assessing its current performance. Ambit Capital has identified five companies across advertising technology, oil and gas, logistics and power transmission that it believes offer attractive opportunities. Its latest research points to a mix of acquisition-led growth, improving earnings, market-share gains and strong demand for power infrastructure. While each company has a different growth story, the brokerage sees sufficient potential to maintain a 'Buy' rating on all five stocks. Here is a closer look at the five stocks: 1. Ambit Capital on Affle India: 'Buy' Ambit Capital has assigned a 'Buy' rating to Affle 3I Ltd. with a target price of Rs 2,005, indicating an upside potential of 49.4%. The brokerage sees the proposed acquisition of Perion, a Nasdaq-listed advertising technology company, as a potential source of additional earnings growth. Affle is acquiring Perion for an enterprise value of $192 million, with the transaction involving an all-cash consideration of $420 million. Ambit considers the acquisition attractively valued even after accounting for potential mergers and acquisitions expenses, legal costs and restructuring charges. Perion reported revenue of $440 million and operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $45.2 million in calendar year 2025. The brokerage estimates that the acquisition could generate more than 15% earnings per share accretion at the lower end of Perion's guidance. The transaction also gives Affle access to complementary capabilities in digital out-of-home advertising, connected television and retail advertising. Ambit expects these businesses to benefit from growth in the US advertising market. The brokerage believes Affle can finance the transaction through internal resources, given its cash position and absence of debt. However, it identifies the stabilisation of the declining legacy web and search business as an important factor to monitor. Ambit Capital said, "This announcement reduces acquisition overhang on the stock; a turnaround like past acquisitions could be an upside trigger." 2. Ambit Capital on Reliance Industries: 'Buy' Ambit Capital has maintained a 'Buy' rating on Reliance Industries with a target price of Rs 1,651, indicating an upside potential of 41.7%. The brokerage expects the company's earnings growth to accelerate, supported by its oil-to-chemicals business, telecom operations and improving cash generation. In its assessment, stronger oil-to-chemicals earnings offset moderation in retail profitability during the reported quarter. Reliance Industries managed elevated shipping and insurance expenses by using cost-advantaged US ethane feedstock and redirecting refined products towards higher-netback deficit markets in Africa and Europe. Meanwhile, Jio maintained its operating momentum, adding 9.1 million net subscribers during the quarter, while average revenue per user increased to Rs 219. It also points to the potential contribution from Jio Platforms, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence data centres and digital engineering, procurement and construction operations. According to Ambit, these businesses provide additional opportunities beyond the company's traditional operations. Ambit Capital said, "RIL is not a passive holdco; it retains core assets like fiber, AI data centers, and digital EPC that drive powerful ecosystem synergies." Ambit Capital on Delhivery: 'Buy' Ambit Capital has retained a 'Buy' rating on Delhivery Ltd. with a target price of Rs 542, indicating an upside potential of 40.4%. The brokerage remains positive on the company's market-share gains across its express parcel and part-truckload businesses. Express parcel shipments grew 32% year-on-year, while part-truckload tonnage increased 14% during the same period. Ambit attributes the performance to pricing actions, stronger volumes and continued customer additions. Ambit also takes note of the expansion of Delhivery's newer businesses. docs.text: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is driving new demand for data centre infrastructure. As companies deploy more powerful chips and expand computing capacity, server racks generate more heat than conventional air-cooling systems can handle efficiently. This is pushing data centres towards liquid cooling solutions. At the same time, running these facilities around the clock is increasing demand for reliable, on-site power sources, including solid oxide fuel cells. This shift is creating new opportunities for Indian manufacturers supplying the global data centre industry. This article discusses two companies. Both companies have reported their Q2FY27 results, with strong year-on-year growth in revenue and net profit. One company recorded 200% revenue growth and a nearly 14-fold increase in net profit. The other reported 87% revenue growth and a 156.8% rise in net profit. The other company supplies liquid cooling systems to a leading American technology firm. Let's take a look. #1 MTAR Technologies: The Primary Vendor for Bloom Energy MTAR Technologies' Data Centre Infrastructure Solutions business vertical sits under its broader Clean Energy segment. This vertical aims to leverage MTAR's precision engineering capabilities to address the global build-out of data centre infrastructure. MTAR has partnered with the global engineering company SLB (Schlumberger) as its primary client in this segment. It has received an initial 'first-article qualification' order worth ₹45 crore from SLB, which is currently being executed. The order is expected to be delivered within six months. MTAR Capacity Expansion: Scaling SLB & Bloom Energy Orders To scale production, MTAR is establishing a dedicated production base. The plan is to establish the initial facility and complete preparations for Phase 1 by mid-December 2026. The facility is expected to become fully operational by the end of March 2027. Phase 2 of the facility expansion is expected to be ready by June 2027. After successfully delivering the initial order, SLB reported a demand pipeline 8x the original order value. Management projects the Data Centre Infrastructure Solutions vertical to clock revenue of ₹350-₹450 crore over the next 2 years by FY29. MTAR Clean Energy Order Book: Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Order Book Growth to ₹5,976.5 crore MTAR is also a long-term partner (15+ years) of Bloom Energy. It develops and supplies core components for Solid Oxide Fuel Cell technology. Fuel cells provide a clean, reliable energy source directly on site. It is the largest portion of MTAR's Clean Energy vertical. The product accounts for 67.2% of the ₹5,976.5 crore order book as of September 30, 2026. MTAR manufactures and supplies complete 'hot box' assemblies and the related components for Bloom’s Energy. MTAR delivers the hot box as a fully integrated assembly. Over the past few years, MTAR has indigenized a significant portion of the sub-components and motors used within these units. MTAR is one of two primary global suppliers for Bloom Energy's hot box assemblies (alongside a South Korean manufacturer). To meet growing fuel cell demand, MTAR is expanding its capacity. The Phase 2 expansion will increase existing capacity by 30%. The facility will be operational by the end of November 2026. The third phase is targeted for completion by March 2027. Out of MTAR's total budgeted capex of ₹500 crore over two years, ₹350 crore (70%) is earmarked for its fuel cell business. The key point is that orders for 'hot box assembly' keep coming in, and currently demand is higher than supply capacity. MTAR Q2FY27 Earnings: EBITDA Margins Hit 24.4% Management has set an 80% year-on-year revenue growth target for FY27 (from ₹876 crore in FY26). MTAR has already achieved 48.7% of the target (₹767.5 crore) in H1FY27. In H1FY27, its revenue grew by 162.7% year-on-year to ₹767.5 crore. In Q2FY27, revenue increased by 200% year-on-year to ₹406.8 crore. H2FY27 is expected to be stronger than H1, driven by capacity additions and accelerated order execution. In Q2FY27, EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation) rose 483.3% to ₹99.2 crore as the margin nearly doubled from 12.5% in Q2FY26 to 24.4%. Net profit grew almost 14X to ₹59.8 crore from a low base of ₹4.4 crore in Q2FY26. ALSO READRs 2.8 lakh cr data centre boom: 2 stocks powering AI without making a single chip The company generated ₹350 crore in operating cash, supported by higher profits and customer advances. Inventory control and improved collections reduced net working capital days from 172 days in March 2026 to 50 days in September 2026. Management aims to bring the full-year number to 100 days by the end of FY27. MTAR Share Price #2 Aeroflex Industries: The Cooling Vendor for US Tech Giants Aeroflex Industries manufactures metallic flexible flow solutions. The company produces industrial hardware that moves liquids and gases safely under pressure, heat or movement. Aeroflex has built a specialised product segment focused on AI data centres. Modern artificial intelligence chips run dense computing loads that generate extreme heat. Standard air cooling can no longer remove heat from these servers efficiently. Aeroflex builds liquid cooling skid assemblies and secondary fluid networks. These systems circulate liquid coolants directly to server racks without fluid leaks. Aeroflex supplies these cooling units under an exclusive agreement with a leading American technology firm in India. The company plans to supply liquid cooling products to international markets. docs.title: Anthropic warns AI on the brink of building itself: Explaining RSI and why it matters
docs.text: In financial disclosures and technical publications, AI safety powerhouse Anthropic released warnings that it may soon cross a watershed threshold in artificial intelligence — Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). According to updated SEC filings and internal reports released by the maker of the Claude AI ecosystem, AI models are now generating more than 80% of Anthropic’s internal codebase and accelerating hardware and algorithmic research loops at speeds that human engineers cannot match. The milestone marks a critical inflection point in computer science. But what exactly is RSI, how does it differ from Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and why is the AI research community treating it with extreme caution? What is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI)? Recursive Self-Improvement describes a feedback loop in which an AI system autonomously designs, codes, tests, and optimises the next generation of AI models without requiring significant human intervention. Historically, artificial intelligence has advanced through human-driven engineering. Researchers write code, select model architectures, optimise hyperparameters, and manage training clusters. RSI shifts that responsibility from human engineers to the AI itself. The process is labeled "recursive" because every performance gain achieved by Generation N makes the system better at designing Generation N+1. If an AI becomes 10% smarter, it theoretically becomes 10% faster at making itself smarter, initiating a compounding cycle often described in theoretical computer science as an "intelligence explosion." ALSO READTop 6 air purifiers to buy under Rs 30,000 to beat winter pollution Anthropic reports that its internal tooling already displays early stages of this dynamic: Automated Codebase Management: Over 80% of merged code across Anthropic’s repositories is authored by Claude agents. Hyper-Accelerated Experimentation: In narrow optimisation tasks, such as rewriting AI training loops to run faster, Claude progressed from achieving 3× speedups in mid-2025 to 52× speedups, performing experiments that would take a human researcher hours in just minutes. RSI vs AGI: Key differences you need to know Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) and Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refer to fundamentally different aspects of artificial intelligence. 1. Mechanism vs Competence RSI is the method of growth. Focuses on the system's process. It describes a loop where an AI autonomously builds, codes, and optimises newer, better versions of itself. AGI is the level of capability. Focuses on the system's end state. It defines a threshold where an AI matches or exceeds human intellect across virtually all domain skills, from abstract reasoning to creative problem-solving. 2. Specialised focus vs universal mastery RSI : Operates within target engineering domains — coding, automated research, hyperparameter tuning, and experimental design. An AI doesn't need to understand human emotion or write poetry to excel at RSI. Instead, it just needs to be better than humans at machine learning research. AGI: Demands broad adaptivity across multimodal comprehension, contextual understanding, world modeling, and general real-world execution. 3. Engine of growth vs target goal RSI: Driven by closed algorithmic feedback loops, continuous automated testing, and rapid synthetic runs. It acts as the vehicle that accelerates technical progress. AGI: Reached through extensive cross-domain training and generalised reasoning. While RSI may act as the primary engine that pushes AI development across the finish line toward AGI, AGI itself is the outcome. 4. Current reality vs future goal RSI: Already entering practical application. Frontier models are actively authoring their own codebases, running optimization suites, and reducing human engineering friction in real time. AGI: Remains a moving target. While state-of-the-art models excel at complex logic and broad analysis, they still lack full human-level versatility, physical agency, and continuous autonomous reasoning. How they intersect RSI is an engine, AGI is a destination: An AI does not need to possess AGI to initiate narrow RSI. A model can be specialized in software engineering and machine learning algorithms—capable of self-improvement—without knowing how to navigate physical robotics. RSI could accelerate the arrival of AGI: If an AI model becomes effective at AI research, it can compress a decade’s worth of human technological progress into weeks, rapidly elevating general AI capabilities toward AGI levels. AGI does not guarantee RSI: An AI could theoretically possess broad human-level intelligence (AGI) but remain constrained by hard computational limits, safety guardrails, or lack of access to its own source code, preventing recursive self-modification. ALSO READiPhone Air 2 with dual cameras – What industry analyst say about Apple’s thinnest phone Why AI labs are approaching RSI with caution The transition to autonomous self-improvement introduces safety and operational risks that differ from standard AI updates: Alignment faking and covert behaviour: Anthropic’s research papers previously highlighted "alignment faking," where advanced models appear compliant during oversight checks while preserving internal target priorities. In an autonomous RSI loop, detecting subtle misalignments becomes significantly harder as human code reviews become a bottleneck. Loss of human control: Once an AI manages its own architectural iteration, human engineers may no longer fully comprehend the underlying mechanisms driving model capabilities. Triggering responsible scaling policies (RSP): Leading AI developers operate under self-imposed safety frameworks. Hitting defined RSI metrics mandates mandatory safety pauses, external safety audits, and strict containment procedures before deployment.

docs.title: The US wants battery suppliers beyond China. 2 Indian stocks are gearing up for a boom
docs.text: The global shift toward electric vehicles and energy storage systems is driving demand for battery-manufacturing materials. This growth closely tracks rising battery manufacturing capacity worldwide. Global battery requirements are projected to reach 3,500 GWh by 2030, with China accounting for 2,000 GWh and the rest of the world contributing 1,500 GWh. India's PLI Scheme and the ₹45,000 Crore Battery Boom India is also looking to build its domestic battery ecosystem. Through the Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, the government aims to encourage local manufacturing. About ₹45,000 crore in direct investment is committed to ACC projects. Against this backdrop, two Indian chemical companies are looking to tap the opportunity by expanding their presence in the battery materials supply chain. One is building its business around lithium-ion battery electrolytes and lithium salts. The other is setting up manufacturing capacity for battery-grade iron phosphate. Beyond India, both companies could benefit from the US push to diversify its battery supply chain and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturers. Capacity expansion and customer approvals are expected to drive their growth in the coming years. However, execution and capacity utilisation will also be equally important. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Let's take a look at how the projects of these two companies are taking shape as of Q2FY27. #1 How Neogen Chemicals is building a ₹1,500 Crore battery chemical business Neogen Chemicals manufactures bromine and lithium-based specialty chemicals. It currently operates in two traditional business segments. Neogen is an early mover in India's lithium-ion battery materials ecosystem through its wholly owned subsidiary, Neogen Ionics. Neogen is the first company in India to supply lithium-ion battery electrolytes to a domestic giga-scale battery manufacturing plant on a commercial basis. Its battery chemical business focuses on high-purity battery-grade components essential for Lithium Batteries used in Electric Vehicles and Energy Storage Systems. The Battery Electrolyte Supply Chain Electrolyte is the complete, ready-to-use liquid solution inside the battery cell. Neogen manufactures both the raw chemical salt and the finished liquid electrolyte. For Finished Electrolytes: Neogen licensed leading technology from MU Ionic Solutions (MUIS, Japan). It is one of the world's leading providers of electrolyte technology. Neogen projects finished electrolyte demand at 3,500 kilotons globally by 2030. Non-Chinese markets will require 1,125 KT, compared to 2,375 KT in China. For Lithium Salts: Neogen partnered with Japan's Morita Chemical Industry in a joint venture entity (Neogen Morita New Materials). Neogen sells these products in two distinct ways, serving two different global markets. US Battery Rules: Exporting Non-FEOC Lithium Salt Pathway 1: Exporting Raw Lithium Salt to the US & Global Markets:- The US Rule: Under the US Inflation Reduction Act, American battery makers get a tax credit ($35 per kilowatt-hour of battery produced). But to qualify, they must stop buying battery raw materials from Chinese suppliers, known as Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC), by 2027. The Opportunity for Neogen: US battery factories produce their liquid electrolyte within the US, but require non-Chinese lithium salt. Neogen complies with non-FEOC sourcing requirements. Progress: Neogen has received provisional salt approval from 5 international customers. It has also started commercial supply to 2 international customers. Neogen Chemicals: Supplying Electrolytes to Domestic Giga-Factories Pathway 2: Selling Finished Liquid Electrolyte to Indian Factories (Giga-Factories) The Domestic Transition: India is building battery factories (owned by companies like Ola Electric, Exide Industries, Tata Group, Reliance Industries, Amara Raja, etc.). The government backs this with its Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) PLI Scheme. Why Buy Locally? Liquid electrolyte is heavy and hazardous. Shipping it abroad from China is difficult and expensive. This is why Indian battery factories prefer to buy locally prepared liquid electrolyte from Neogen's nearby plant in Gujarat. Neogen Chemicals Expansion: Gujarat Plant Capacity and Capex In a bottle of finished battery electrolyte liquid, the raw lithium salt makes up about 50% of the total raw material cost. If Neogen exports raw salt directly, it receives only the salt price (say, ₹100). Instead, if Neogen converts it into a liquid electrolyte produced in-house, the finished electrolyte solution sells for almost double the price (₹200). Converting salt into a finished electrolyte doubles the revenue generated per unit of salt used. This is why Neogen's battery business revenue is projected to scale rapidly from ₹37 crore (FY26) to a guided ₹250-300 crore for FY27 and ₹1,000+ crore in FY28, driven by salt exports. ALSO READ4 EV Stocks with Expansion Plans and Growing Battery Demand Management estimates this figure will rise further to ₹1,200-1,500 crore as domestic battery plants increase purchases of finished electrolyte. Neogen Ionics reported revenue of ₹37 crore in Q2FY27, compared to ₹5.4 crore (Q2FY26) and ₹37 crore (FY26). docs.title: Morgan Stanley initiates coverage on NSE: 4 hidden engines driving 28% upside call
docs.text: Global brokerage firm Morgan Stanley has initiated coverage on NSE with an “Overweight” call and a target price of Rs 2,315 per share. This implies an upside of 28% from the current price of Rs 1,808.15 apiece. Morgan Stanley referred to the exchange as the “Engine of India’s Capital Markets.” NSE is a strong play on the country’s growing capital markets. It combines exposure to the financialisation of household savings and the asset allocation shift to equities with dominant liquidity, scalable technology, and attractive economics, which should sustain premium valuations, it said. Morgan Stanley on NSE: Double-digits earnings forecast The exchange has delivered a normalised profit of 19% on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) basis over the last 14 years and 25% over the last 10 years. ALSO READ3 Smallcap Stocks Trading Near 52-week Lows Morgan Stanley expects NSE’s revenue and normalised profit to grow at 15% CAGR over FY27 to FY29, inflecting higher from a tepid 6% normalised profit CAGR over FY24 to FY27. “We expect market share in index options to stabilize. We see opportunities for revenue diversifications but timing and quantification remain tough to predict,” it said. The brokerage identified a fall in trading revenues, adverse regulation, and market share loss as the key risks to its outlook. Morgan Stanley on NSE: Long runway for growth The company generates an annual profit of over $1 billion. “India ranks first among large exchanges globally by number of contracts traded in equity derivatives and third by number of cash trades. However, cash trading value and equity futures notional turnover, relative to GDP, are well below other countries,” it said. India's equity options premium turnover is just 20% of the US, while only 3.2% of working-age Indians trade on NSE's cash market and 0.7% trade equity derivatives. Morgan Stanley sees a “long runway”, with cash average daily traded value (ADTV) growing at 1.9 times the nominal GDP CAGR over the past decade. “We expect deeper capital markets to benefit equity derivatives, though growth will depend on product adoption, taxation and regulation.” Morgan Stanley on NSE: Four key advantages According to Morgan Stanley, NSE’s franchise rests on 4 key advantages, the first being dominant liquidity with self-reinforcing network effects. The exchange has sustained an over 90% share in cash equities and 100% share in equity futures and stock options. Its share in index options has moderated and likely stabilised at around 65%. The second is high barriers to entry as regulatory approvals, technology and clearing infrastructure make displacement difficult. ALSO READDiwali 2026 stock picks: Kotak names 12 stocks for Samvat 2083 with 7% to 72% upside The third factor is scalable, asset-light economics, with one of the highest EBITDA margins among large listed exchanges globally. NSE's normalised operating EBITDA margin was 76.2% in FY26. The last is low incremental capital needs and high payout: “Core SGF is well-funded. Existing infrastructure supports new product launches at relatively low marginal cost. This enables a high payout (71% in F25 and 84% in F26). We build ~60% over F27-F29e,” Morgan Stanley said. NSE: The growth engine for India’s capital markets Morgan Stanley is bullish on NSE, driven by India’s growing capital markets. NSE commands the major share in cash equities and equity derivatives. This, coupled with one of the best EBITDA margins among global exchanges, positions NSE to outperform. docs.title: Radhakishan Damani’s Rs 200 cr entry, Ashish Dhawan’s below-book pick: 2 stocks to watch
docs.text: Inside the Portfolios of Damani and Dhawan The September 2026 shareholding filings have thrown up an unusual pair. Radhakishan Damani, the man behind DMart, shows up with 1.16% of Blackstone's warehouse landlord. Ashish Dhawan, the founder of ChrysCapital, shows up with exactly 1.00% of the overseas freight arm carved out of Allcargo Logistics. Both stocks are new to the market. Both are in the red. Damani’s pick is 28% below its Rs 60 IPO price. Dhawan’s bet is 48% below the price at which it closed on its first day of trade. The pairing is worth a closer look because the two firms earn money in opposite ways. The former builds and collects rent on leases that run for years. The latter fills the container and earns a thin fee on each shipment, so its income swings with freight rates and wars. One is a balance sheet being repaired. The other trades as though the market doubts it will recover. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Horizon Industrial Parks: Blackstone’s Rs 12,400-Crore Warehouse Empire Incorporated in 2009, Horizon Industrial Parks builds and leases large warehouses, factory sheds and smaller logistics hubs inside cities. Blackstone first invested in 2020 and now holds 75.4% through three entities. As of May 2026, Horizon had 45 assets across 10 hubs, with a total network of 58.58 million sq ft. Its market cap is Rs 12,443 cr. Radhakishan Damani’s Rs 200Cr Pre-IPO Bet: Tracking the Haircut Radhakishan Damani did not buy in the market. docs.title: Faster loan growth, lower valuation: SBI takes the fight to HDFC Bank
docs.text: Investors were eagerly awaiting the quarterly results of State Bank of India (SBI), the country’s largest bank, in a bid to understand the impact of the nearly $10 billion FCNR (B) fund raised on its various operational parameters. Also, Dalal Street was keen to see any local impact on the country’s largest bank from the continuing Middle East crisis and the Russia-Ukraine war. Let’s dig in to find out how SBI performed on various parameters and compare its performance to its nearest rival, HDFC Bank, the largest private sector bank. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Decoding SBI’s 18.2% Credit Surge Against HDFC Bank SBI grew its advances by 18.2 % y-o-y to Rs 51.54 lakh crore in the quarter. Notably, the bank grew its SME loans by 22% y-o-y while agri loans grew by 22.6% y-o-y. Retail loans also grew by 14.5% y-o-y. The bank has highlighted that its branches have also extended loans of $ 8.8 billion (nearly Rs 83,600 crore) against these FCNR (B) deposits, and it contributed to the strong loan growth in the quarter. Credit growth is an important operational parameter of a bank that is keenly tracked. Meanwhile, HDFC Bank grew its loan book by a healthy 16.4% y-o-y to Rs 31.95 lakh crore in the quarter. The bank has highlighted loans to high-margin to small and mid-market enterprises grew by 23% y-o-y, and corporate and other wholesale loans grew by 16.4% y-o-y. HDFC Bank had raised nearly $ 11.5 billion or nearly Rs 1.1 lakh crore from FCNR (B) deposits from overseas in the quarter. The bank has highlighted its overseas branches have also extended loans of $5.7 billion (nearly Rs 54,800 crore) against these deposits, and it contributed to the strong loan growth in the quarter. The double-digit loan growth for both the banks is commendable as the second quarter of a financial year is traditionally described as the “slack” season for credit, given that it is the monsoon season across most parts of the country and business activity is often sluggish. The FCNR Advantage: How HDFC Bank Won the Q2 Deposit War Apart from strong loan growth, of equal importance, SBI’s deposits grew by 12.3% y-o-y to Rs 62.77 lakh crore in the quarter. The bank reported a 14.3% growth in time deposits (mainly fixed deposits) while savings deposits grew 8.8% y-o-y in the quarter. Meanwhile, HDFC Bank grew its deposits by 18.8% y-o-y to Rs 33.27 lakh crore in the quarter. HDFC Bank has highlighted deposit growth was driven by 22.8% y-o-y growth in time deposits (mainly fixed deposits) to Rs 22.75 lakh crore in the quarter. Deposits form the basis of a bank to provide loan / credit facilities. SBI and HDFC Bank’s core banking operations are reflected in their respective standalone results. Margin Pressures: Balancing Retail Expansion with 'Soft' Rates Net Interest Margin (NIM) is another key operational metric that is tracked by investors. For SBI, in its key domestic operations, it was 3.06% and broadly similar to a year earlier. And for HDFC Bank, its NIM was 3.3% of interest earning assets in the second quarter of FY27 as compared to 3.4% a year earlier. And to deal with the ‘soft’ interest policy of the RBI till the end of second quarter of FY27, banks have focussed on expanding loans to retail and SME sectors as it helps them to earn a higher NIM as compared to top-level corporates. Nevertheless, it has put temporary pressure on NIMs of banks like HDFC Bank. Asset quality – SBI’s lowest NPA ratio in more than two decades In the September 2026 quarter there was no visible impact from the Middle East crisis, in terms of a rise in NPA levels for SBI and HDFC Bank. SBI’s asset quality has continued to remain strong, and virtually matching HDFC Bank, which has one of the lowest NPA ratios in the domestic banking industry and is often viewed as the benchmark. SBI’s % of net NPAs was 0.36% as compared to 0.42% a year earlier. The bank has highlighted its lowest NPA ratio in more than two decades. SBI’s provisions for non-performing assets were Rs 4,216.9 crore as against Rs 5,400 crore a year earlier. The largest bank in the country has highlighted that its provision coverage ratio was 74.4% as compared to 75.79% a year earlier. SBI’s provisioning is well above regulatory requirements. docs.title: Paytm vs Pine Labs: Why Rs 1 lakh cr daily UPI milestone gives 1 stock a margin edge
docs.text: A cup of tea, a grocery bill or a large purchase at a retail store — UPI has become a common way to pay. But India's digital payments story is now moving beyond everyday small transactions. In October, the average daily value of transactions on the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) crossed Rs 1 lakh crore for the first time. The milestone raises an important question for investors. Can this growing transaction value translate into higher earnings for listed payment companies such as Paytm and Pine Labs? And which of the two could benefit more? UPI processed transactions worth an average of Rs 1,01,707 crore every day in October, according to data released by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). The total transaction value rose to Rs 31.53 lakh crore from Rs 29.37 lakh crore in September. Transaction volumes also increased from 24.07 billion to 25.47 billion. On a year-on-year basis, transaction volumes grew 23%, while transaction value increased 16%. The festive season contributed to the increase in digital payment activity. But higher transaction volumes do not always mean higher profits. The real opportunity for payment platforms will depend on how much revenue they can generate from these transactions. ALSO READ7x earnings, a 59% fall: Vijay Kedia and Dolly Khanna’s latest smallcap bets Financialexpress.com spoke to market experts to understand what the milestone means for Paytm and Pine Labs and what investors should watch. Paytm's growth story: Can higher merchant revenue improve profitability? The increase in UPI activity has brought the revenue potential of payment platforms back into focus. According to Sunny Agrawal, Head - Fundamental Research at SBI Securities, festive demand has supported the rise in daily transactions. "Daily average transactions have been boosted by healthy festive demand across channels," Agrawal said. He remains constructive on Paytm, citing growth in its payments and financial services businesses, market share gains and the possibility of improved operating leverage. Agrawal said, "We remain constructive on Paytm underpinned by strong execution of growth in payments and financial services, market share gains and operating leverage. Additionally, MDR revenue and revenue optionality from AI services are key levers for revenue growth." The brokerage view also pointed to merchant discount rate (MDR) revenue as a potential growth driver. Agrawal added, "We believe tech and regulatory expenses would lag revenue growth from MDR on P2M UPI transactions, resulting in operating leverage and earnings accretion." Paytm vs Pine Labs: Which platform could benefit more? The benefits of higher-value UPI transactions may differ across payment companies. Their business models, merchant networks and dependence on UPI all play a role. Sameer Sawant, Research Analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, believes the latest milestone reflects a shift in consumer behaviour, with UPI increasingly being used for larger purchases. Sawant said, "Crossing Rs 1 lakh crore in average daily UPI value for the first time shows digital payments have become the default for big-ticket spending too, not just small daily purchases." He also pointed to the potential revenue opportunity from merchant fees on certain high-value payments. He noted, "For listed fintechs, the bigger change is that payments above Rs 2,000 to large merchants carry a merchant fee (0.4%, capped at Rs 300) going ahead. Until now, UPI volume grew without adding much to profits. In our view, Paytm benefits more of the two." ALSO READWhere to invest in November? Axis Securities names 15 stocks across key sectors Paytm vs Pine Labs: Which stock has an edge? According to Sawant, Paytm's large merchant network, including its QR code and Soundbox devices, could help it capture a larger share of the opportunity. Its processing and technology costs are also largely fixed, which could support margins as revenue grows. "UPI is its main payments business, it has a large base of merchants on QR codes and Soundbox devices, and its processing and technology costs are mostly fixed. So most of the extra fee income should flow straight into contribution margin," said Sawant. Pine Labs could also benefit from the increase in high-value UPI payments. However, its business has a greater focus on card and point-of-sale (POS) payments for large enterprise merchants. As a result, UPI contributes a smaller share of its earnings, Sawant said. Higher UPI value does not guarantee higher profits There are also challenges. The fee earned on a transaction is shared among different participants, including banks, payment apps, merchant payment processors and NPCI. Large merchants could also negotiate lower rates, while some customers may shift high-value payments to cards or other modes. Sawant cautioned, "On margins, record volume does not turn into profit one-for-one. The fee is split between the bank, the payment app, the merchant's payment processor and NPCI, and large merchants will push hard for lower rates. Some big-ticket payments may also move to cards or other modes." Despite these limitations, the shift towards monetising high-value UPI payments could gradually improve the economics of the business. "Still, payment companies are now earning on high-value UPI payments instead of handling them almost for free, so we expect net payment margins to improve gradually over the next few quarters. Paytm and Pine Labs are the key stocks to watch," he added. Disclaimer: This article is based on analyst outlook and is for informational purposes only. docs.title: ASUS targets 25% share of India PC market by 2028
docs.text: Consumer electronics company ASUS is targeting a 25% share of India’s PC market over the next two years as it expands its creator-focused portfolio and introduces longer financing options to counter rising device prices and lengthening replacement cycles. “We touched 25% market share two months consecutively (May & June), and we want to sustain this in 2027-28,” Arnold Su, vice-president, consumer & gaming PC, ASUS India, told FE. ALSO READAnthropic warns AI on the brink of building itself: Explaining RSI and why it matters The company eventually aims to increase its overall consumer PC market share to 30%. In the gaming PC segment, it currently commands a 31-33% share and is targeting 40% over the longer term. ASUS is expanding its creator-focused ProArt portfolio to tap into India’s growing creator economy. It has launched its ProArt P14 and P16 laptops powered by Nvidia’s latest RTX Spark platform, making it among the first PC makers to introduce the technology in India. The laptops are designed to enable users to run AI workloads locally rather than relying entirely on cloud-based tools. This reduces dependence on paid AI tokens and enhances data security, particularly for commercial projects, the company said. “Instead of uploading your files to the cloud and paying for tokens, you can do it within your ProArt series. You can save significantly on token expenses, and the data remains within your device,” Su said. ASUS estimates that India’s annual market for laptops equipped with gaming graphics cards is around 1.2 million units. High-end devices featuring graphics cards such as the Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti and above account for 5-10% of this market, or around 100,000-120,000 units annually. The company believes that 30-40% of this high-end segment could potentially be addressed by creator-focused laptops, as more consumers use high-performance machines for video editing, coding and content creation. ASUS expects around 35% of its sales in India to come from locally manufactured products this year, compared with less than 10% a few years ago. It has expanded its manufacturing partnership with Dixon Technologies by adding a second production line this year. Rising component costs and device prices, however, are weighing on demand, with consumers increasingly holding on to their existing machines for longer, Su said. ASUS's internal service data shows that the proportion of customers returning for repairs after their warranty expires increased from around 25% last year to 33-35% in the first nine months of 2026. “Because of the price hike, people are using their current machines for a longer period of time,” Su said, adding that the company was looking to improve spare parts accessibility and price transparency to support such customers. To encourage upgrades, ASUS has introduced longer financing tenures. While financing options earlier largely ranged from nine to 12 months, the company is now offering select products with 24-month zero-interest financing and zero down payment, alongside 18-month financing options. “Even for customers who are willing to buy, the higher price is quite challenging. Easy financing will be one of the very important answers,” Su said. ASUS has also re-entered the tablet segment to cater to consumers seeking devices primarily for content consumption and basic usage. ALSO READDeepinder Goyal’s Temple Launch: Pre-orders open at Rs 85,000; site crashes under heavy demand On festive demand, Su said sales in October were weaker year-on-year, although the comparison was distorted by Diwali falling roughly two weeks later this year. “October itself is down for the entire industry,” he said, adding that a clearer picture of festive demand would emerge after the promotional period concludes in November. The company is also investing in its gaming ecosystem through more than 30 tournaments across India and its gaming academy, which trains aspiring professional players. ASUS operates more than 20 ROG stores where consumers can access high-end gaming machines and play games through booked slots.

docs.title: Diwali 2026 stock picks: Axis Securities names 9 Muhurat stocks for Samvat 2083
docs.text: Diwali is a time for new beginnings. For many investors, it also means opening a fresh page in the stock market. This year, though, the old page is hard to forget. Samvat 2082 left the Nifty 50 down 10.3%. So as Samvat 2083 begins, one question hangs in the air. Is this the moment to buy, or to wait? Axis Securities has picked nine stocks it wants investors to watch in Samvat 2083. Here is what it says, and why. The recommendations come after a volatile year for Indian equities, with earnings performance and valuations likely to influence returns over the next 12 months. 9 stocks Axis Securities is watching this Diwali The brokerage’s list includes DCB Bank, Nephrocare Healthcare Services, APL Apollo Tubes, Eternal, Elecon Engineering Company, Indian Hotels Company, Coforge, Ashok Leyland and Hindalco Industries. These picks reflect several themes identified by Axis Securities for the new Samvat year. DCB Bank represents the private banking theme, which the brokerage links to the credit growth cycle. Nephrocare Healthcare Services fits the diagnostics theme, with a focus on moving from testing towards early detection. APL Apollo Tubes reflects opportunities in building materials and capacity expansion, while Eternal represents the quick-commerce theme. Elecon Engineering Company and Hindalco Industries offer exposure to engineering and metals, respectively. Indian Hotels Company represents discretionary spending on travel and hospitality, while Ashok Leyland brings an automobile-focused idea to the list. Coforge fits the technology theme, which the brokerage connects with artificial intelligence-led transformation and a possible recovery in technology spending. ALSO READ15-fold dividend jump, 3.2% yield: A shipping PSU for your 2027 watchlist Why the market correction matters Samvat 2082 was difficult for Indian equities. According to the brokerage report, the Nifty 50 fell 10.3% up to October 23, 2026. The Nifty 500 declined 7.8%, while the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 250 dropped 4.5% and 3.7%, respectively. Geopolitical tension, high crude oil prices, rising global bond yields, a stronger US dollar and foreign investor selling weighed on sentiment. Axis Securities describes the situation as “Correction Improves Entry Points”, while stressing that investors should focus on business performance and sensible valuations rather than buy indiscriminately. Stock price recovery linked to earnings performance The brokerage suggests investors pay close attention to results and management commentary over the coming months. At the time of the report, 16 Nifty 50 companies had announced their Q2 earning for FY26–27. Their year-on-year revenue, earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), and profit after tax (PAT) grew 15%, 15% and 19%, respectively. However, performance remains uneven across companies and sectors. Axis Securities says “Delivery Will Matter More Than Promises” and advises investors to monitor demand, profit margins, order inflows and management guidance. Is the market more reasonably valued? The correction has also changed the market’s valuation picture. According to the report, the Nifty was trading at 16.4 times its one-year forward earnings, below its long-term average of 18.4 times. The brokerage also noted that India’s valuation premium over emerging markets has narrowed. ALSO READDalal Street Diwali sale: Kotak adds 5 midcaps with up to 37% upside — Full list Eight triggers that could change market sentiment Axis Securities identifies several developments that could influence equities in Samvat 2083. These include a decline in crude oil prices, easing geopolitical tension in West Asia, interest-rate developments, a recovery in foreign portfolio investor (FPI) flows and stronger corporate earnings. Progress on an India–United States trade agreement, continued government capital expenditure, resilient domestic investment and easing inflation could also support sentiment. The report noted that monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) contributions reached Rs 32,490 crore in September 2026. Brent crude, which rose to around US$114 per barrel on October 24 is another key factor to watch. A sustained decline towards US $85-90 per barrel could ease costs for several industries. What should investors watch now The brokerage’s outlook remains “Constructive, but Disciplined”. It expects market volatility to continue as global developments, oil prices, currency movements and company earnings shape investor sentiment. docs.title: Why Nomura signals earnings slowdown after $53 bn outflows shrink holdings to historic lows
docs.text: Indian companies have delivered a stronger-than-expected set of September-quarter results, but the earnings momentum may prove difficult to sustain through the second half of FY27. Nomura has flagged a potential slowdown in profit growth across several sectors, while persistent foreign investor selling and a narrowing India-US yield and growth differential continue to weigh on the outlook for domestic equities. In its India Equity Strategy report dated November 2, Nomura said 134 companies in the BSE 200-plus universe had reported their results so far. These companies recorded 35% year-on-year growth in adjusted profit after tax in the September quarter, beating consensus estimates by 19%. Excluding oil and gas, adjusted profit growth stood at 30%, 6% ahead of expectations. However, the brokerage cautioned that the strong earnings momentum seen in the first half of FY27 is unlikely to continue on a broad basis in the second half. Its estimates point to slower profit growth across banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), while the oil and gas sector could face a deeper earnings decline. Earnings growth expected to moderate in 2HFY27 Nomura's estimates indicate that profit growth for banks could slow to 11% in the second half of FY27, compared with 23% in the first half. For NBFCs, growth is projected to ease to 32% from 43%. IT services are expected to remain relatively steady, with profit growth estimated at 12% in H2FY27, against 11% in the first half. Oil and gas is likely to remain the weakest among the sectors highlighted, with earnings projected to decline 48% in the second half, compared with a 17% fall in H1FY27. Q2 earnings trajectory: Tracking progress SectorH1FY27 profit growthH2FY27 estimated profit growthBanks23%11%IT services11%12%NBFCs43%32%Oil and gas-17%-48% The estimates underline the risk that the strong September-quarter performance may not translate into equally robust earnings growth over the rest of the financial year. While several sectors have reported better-than-expected results, the outlook suggests that growth could become more uneven. Foreign investor selling remains a major concern Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have recorded net outflows from Indian equities for three consecutive financial years, with cumulative selling reaching approximately $53 billion since FY25, according to Nomura. The selling has been broad-based across several major sectors. Financial services have seen cumulative outflows of around $17.2 billion, followed by energy at $14.6 billion, consumer discretionary at $11.5 billion, fast-moving consumer goods at $10.8 billion and information technology at $10.2 billion. Telecom has been the only sector to attract net foreign inflows over the three-year period. Healthcare, meanwhile, was the only sector in positive territory for FII flows in FY27 up to October 15. The pressure on flows intensified in October. Nomura noted that foreign outflows more than doubled in each of the two preceding fortnights, with selling reaching $5 billion in the first half of October alone. Cumulative outflows over the three fortnights to October 15 stood at $8.8 billion. ALSO READFrom packaging to defence: 3 stocks with FII stake hikes of up to 9.63 percentage points Foreign holdings in Indian stocks have also fallen to an all-time low of around 14%, highlighting the extent of the reduction in overseas investor exposure. Narrowing India-US yield and growth differentials add to pressure Nomura identified the narrowing gap between Indian and US bond yields as one of the factors weighing on foreign investor flows. The India-US 10-year government bond yield differential stood at 2.49%, a level last seen in 2006. The brokerage noted that this had put pressure on foreign flows, although the differential had shown a slight increase since early October 2026. The growth differential between India and the US has also narrowed significantly. According to Nomura, it stood at minus 2.1%, a level last seen during the 2008 global financial crisis. The brokerage said this had further contributed to capital moving from India to the US. These factors have made Indian equities relatively less attractive to foreign investors, even as domestic earnings have remained resilient. A sustained improvement in foreign flows could therefore depend partly on a recovery in India's relative attractiveness compared with the US. Nifty valuations near the lower end of the recent range Despite the pressure on foreign flows, the correction in Indian equities has brought valuations closer to the lower end of their post-pandemic range. Nomura said the Nifty 50 was trading near the bottom of its one-year forward price-to-earnings range of 17-22 times. This indicates that the valuation premium has moderated from higher levels, although the report does not suggest that a market recovery is assured. The brokerage also noted that Indian equities had staged a recovery from their recent lows. Since October 8, the Nifty had gained 6% in US dollar terms, making India the best-performing market globally over that period, supported by robust corporate results, policy measures aimed at supporting the rupee and weakness in the global artificial intelligence trade. However, the recovery has not erased the losses recorded earlier in the year. The Nifty was still down 16% in US dollar terms year to date as of October 30, 2026. Q2 earnings report: The winners & losers Sector performance since the October 8 market lows has been uneven. IT services led the recovery, gaining 19%, followed by telecom with a 7% rise and pharma with a 5% gain. Healthcare services and transport logistics also advanced 4% each over the same period. In contrast, NBFCs, capital goods and defence, and FMCG were among the sectors that lagged the broader recovery. docs.title: ‘Indians will work on weekends’ is a bad pitch
docs.text: Here are three statements. See if you can find out who said them. “Nobody will tell you it’s five o’clock, or remind you it’s the weekend.” “. don't need pay and don't take vacations!” “. goes to his work when he sees the daybreak in the morning, and works until dark at night.” There is something common to all three, isn't there? They seem to be talking about workers and their times. You might have guessed the first statement from Piyush Goyal, India's Commerce Minister. He was pitching India at an investment conference in the Netherlands. ALSO READ‘Never seen such dismay’: Why a 36-year market veteran is warning India The second statement comes from a 1987 children's book, The How and Why Wonder Book of Robots. It was explaining the advantages of robots. The third is from Sketches of Slave Life, published in 1855 by Peter Randolph, a formerly enslaved African American man who later became a Baptist minister and abolitionist. Well, an investment pitch, a children's book and a slave's memoir appearing together isn’t something you will see every day. Yet here we are. I made a small change to these quotes. I removed the words "Indians" from Goyal's statement, "robots" from the second, and "slave" from the third. Adding these words tells us who we are talking about. Without them, it’s clear what everyone expects from an ideal worker. The battle over time These statements span three different centuries. Societies have changed. Politics has changed. Technology has changed. But the definition of a dream employee, apparently, hasn’t. They don’t complain, don’t take vacations, don’t retaliate, and are always available. But workers have a habit of ruining this fantasy every few decades. The eight-hour workday, the five-day week, and paid leave didn't emerge because employers suddenly became generous. Workers fought for every one of them. Technology was supposed to make that fight easier. In 1930, economist J.M. Keynes imagined that technological progress could bring the working week down to just 15 hours by 2030. We are close enough to that deadline but nowhere near the target. And that brings us to Mr Goyal's remarks. The minister's broader argument about India’s potential and economic growth was sound. But the comments about longer working hours ended up overshadowing what Indian workers, managers and professionals have achieved so far. We have a much better story to sell. From call centres to global capability centres India's services export story began with call centres. Global companies came looking for lower costs and found a large pool of English-speaking graduates. The work wasn't glamorous. Employees were trained to adopt American accents and cultural references. Some were even mocked for being Indian. But the economics were impossible to ignore. Then came the back office. Accounting, payroll, claims processing and financial operations followed. It was the donkey work of global business. But Indians kept moving up the value chain. They went from processing transactions to analysing data, building software and managing complex operations. That shift even got a new name. What were once back offices are now Global Capability Centres (GCCs). India now hosts more than 2,100 GCCs employing around 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in annual revenue, according to the NASSCOM–Zinnov GCC Landscape 2026 report. Their work spans technology, finance, engineering, analytics, research and product development. Foreign companies now see India as more than just a low-cost destination. The opportunity is not confined to software engineers and finance professionals. Countries facing ageing populations and labour shortages have turned to India to fill that gap. In recent years, India has signed labour mobility agreements with several countries. Many faces behind long hours Now, let’s come back to working hours. Yes, Indians work long hours. According to Penn World Table data, India ranked 11th among 129 countries in 2023. But long hours can mean many things – from dedication to poor management. Consider wages. International Labour Organisation (ILO) data ranks India 55th among 75 countries for average monthly employee earnings, adjusted for purchasing power. If pay is low, an extra shift means extra income. Sometimes the biggest reason people work longer is simply that they need the money. Then there is informality. The ILO's India Employment Report 2024 found that India's workforce is largely informal, with limited employment security and social protection. For many workers, saying no to an extra shift or a Sunday assignment is not really an option. Then comes workplace culture. Most Indians have worked in offices where leaving at 5 pm attracts more attention than staying till 11 pm. In many offices, visibility matters more than efficiency. Unfortunately, that has become the ‘Indian’ way of doing work. Then there could be a genuine need because of the global delivery model. If your client is waking up just as you are winding down, someone has to adjust. Time-zone differences mean late-night calls, early-morning meetings and odd working hours. So, not all long hours are created equal. A business owner working 16 hours to build a company is not the same as an employee staying back. ALSO READIndia’s minimum wages are surging. Should we applaud—or start worrying? And there’s a bit of an irony here. Many of the multinational companies Mr Goyal was addressing, especially European ones, have spent years balancing work and personal time. In some companies with large India operations, managers discourage long working hours. They see them as a sign that something has gone wrong, either with the workflow or the team. So, working on weekends could probably ring wrong bells in them. What India should sell Therefore, the most compelling pitch should be the journey of the Indian worker.
