docs.title: Grain ethanol firms push for price revision
docs.text: Grain-based ethanol manufacturers have urged the Centre to review procurement prices and allocation norms for the 2026-27 supply year, warning that restrictions on sugar-based feedstocks could disrupt supplies and undermine the viability of maize-based distilleries. The government has barred oil marketing companies (OMCs) from procuring ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses for the November 2026-October 2027 supply year. ALSO READSugar output may fall in 2026-27, no ethanol diversion: Industry "The procurement price for maize-based ethanol had been cut from Rs 71.86/litre to Rs 68.86/litre, would hit the financial viability of corn-based distilleries and farmers' income," CK Jain, president, Grain Ethanol Manufacturers' Association (GEMA), told FE. Jain said the latest tender placed a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly FCI's surplus foodgrain, priced at Rs 60.32 per litre, and damaged foodgrains, priced at Rs 64 per litre. This, he said, could weaken maize's role in the biofuel sector. Industry sources said the price differential had created uncertainty over the distribution of procurement demand, particularly as maize prices had risen sharply to around Rs 27 per kg from Rs 18 per kg a year ago. GEMA is also concerned that maize may not receive an adequate share of procurement under the OMCs' lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. The industry estimates that ethanol production from damaged foodgrains and broken rice could rise substantially, with the combined volume projected to increase from an estimated 800 million litres last year to more than 7,000 million litres in the current ethanol supply year. “Broken rice supply will be crucial as historically its contribution towards ethanol manufacturing has never increased beyond 1000 million litres,” Jain said. Industry representatives fear that increased competition from broken-rice ethanol, priced at Rs 64 per litre, could force maize-based producers to lower their prices, eventually putting pressure on the prices farmers receive for maize. The food ministry had earlier said that the inclusion of maize as a feedstock for ethanol production had helped provide farmers with an assured market and better prices. During the 2024-25 ethanol supply year, 13.11 million tonne of maize was used for ethanol production, compared with nearly 5 million tonne of broken rice and surplus rice supplied by the FCI. Last month, state-owned Bharat Petroleum Corporation, on behalf of the OMCs, invited bids for 11,000 million litres of ethanol for the 2026-27 supply year to meet the target of blending 20% ethanol with petrol. The tender permits bids for ethanol produced from maize, broken rice, FCI's surplus rice and C-heavy molasses, which has a lower sugar content. The exclusion of sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses follows the government's directive to halt the diversion of sugar towards ethanol production amid concerns over a possible decline in sugarcane output and sugar production. The OMCs have extended the deadline for submitting bids for the 2026-27 supply year to November 5 from October 29, 2026. ALSO READExplainer: Why motorists don’t want ethanol in their fuel tanks Industry estimates suggest that in the 2025-26 supply year, only 2,750 million litres, or around 26% of the total ethanol requirement, came from sugar-based feedstocks. Grain-based sources accounted for 7,610 million litres, or 74%t, comprising 5,180 million litres from maize and 3,050 million litres from rice. Industry sources estimate that 2025-26 ESY, only 2,750 million litres of ethanol, about 26% of the total requirement, was sourced from sugar-based feedstocks, compared to 7,610 million litres (74%) from grain-based sources—5,180 million litres from maize (47%) and 3,050 million litres from rice (27%). The FCI diverts surplus rice for ethanol production after meeting requirements under the National Food Security Act, other welfare schemes and maintaining the prescribed buffer stock. It had stopped supplying rice for ethanol production during the 2022-23 supply year.

docs.title: Crude oil prices slide over 6% on US-Iran diplomatic hopes: Is the supply threat over?
docs.text: Global crude oil prices fell sharply on Monday after new signals from the US and Iran raised hopes of a diplomatic resolution to their ongoing conflict. Comments by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that President Donald Trump preferred a peaceful solution rather than military action brought some relief to an oil market worried about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 6.07% to $106.54 per barrel; however, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude declined 6.2% to $97.65 per barrel as of 8:55 am ET, according to CNBC. The decline came after oil prices had climbed to their highest level in six months at the end of October, showing concerns that the conflict could intensify after the November 3 US midterm elections. Why are oil prices falling now, and does this mean the threat to global oil supplies is over? Let us take a closer look. What triggered the fall in crude oil prices? The immediate trigger was a change in expectations around the possibility of further US military action against Iran. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump preferred to resolve the conflict through diplomacy, although the president had not ruled out military action. ALSO READGoldman Sachs raises Brent Dec target to $105: Why $27 risk premium may push oil to $130 “The president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful,” Rubio told reporters. “But we would prefer to do it peacefully.” President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Salina Regional Airport, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina Kan. (AP Photo) The comments indicated that Washington was willing to give diplomatic efforts more time before considering another military offensive. This comment is important to oil markets because any fresh military escalation involving Iran could threaten oil production and shipments from the wider Middle East. Investors had factored in the possibility of further attacks, particularly after reports suggested that the US was preparing for potential military action after the midterm elections. However, the possibility of negotiations reduced some of these immediate concerns. Why does the US-Iran conflict affect global oil prices? The Middle East is one of the world's most important oil-producing regions. Any conflict that threatens oil production, refineries or shipping routes in the region can affect the amount of crude available in the global market.One of the biggest concerns is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. It is a critical route for international oil shipments, with a significant share of the world's seaborne oil trade passing through it. When tensions rise in the region, attacks on oil tankers or restrictions on shipping through the strait can delay supplies and make transportation more expensive. Even the possibility of disruptions can push prices higher because traders worry about whether enough oil will be available in the coming weeks and months. The Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, has already affected energy supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that global oil inventories have fallen significantly since the war disrupted shipments. Chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) told CNBC that the world had drained nearly 1 billion barrels from inventories since the conflict began. This explains why oil prices had remained elevated even before the latest developments. ALSO READ$50 bn Arabian Sea corridor could rewrite Gulf energy security — but it’s still just talk Are diplomatic talks between the US and Iran making progress? There are signs that both sides are still open to negotiations, although a final agreement remains uncertain. According to Al Jazeera, Iranian authorities indicated that a deal was still possible following two days of talks mediated by Qatar. However, Tehran said any agreement would have to be implemented in practice rather than remain limited to promises. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi also said on Sunday that the purpose of the discussions was to continue consultations with Qatari mediators. He added that Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". Trading Economics reported that Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said the country's supreme leader had approved the government's pursuit of talks aimed at ending the conflict. Meanwhile, Trump reportedly told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he wanted to give diplomacy more time before considering renewed military action. These developments have helped reduce immediate concerns among oil traders. However, diplomatic discussions do not necessarily mean that the conflict is close to ending. Why are oil prices still vulnerable regardless of Monday's fall? The risks to global oil supplies have not disappeared yet. Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicated that the US was preparing for possible renewed military action after the November 3 midterm elections. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei also called on the country's armed forces on Saturday to respond to “any level or type of threat” with “an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response.” Oil supplies from the Persian Gulf fell sharply after the conflict broke out (Reuters) There are also concerns about attacks on oil tankers and energy infrastructure across the Middle East. Reuters reported that attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz had increased recently. However, there were also signs that shipments from some major oil exporters were recovering. Saudi Arabia's crude exports increased in October compared with September, despite attacks by Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, according to two of three ship-tracking companies cited by Reuters. docs.title: Financing urban transition
docs.text:
Sign In 
 CLOSE 
 For uninterrupted reading, switch to App
 READ IN APP 
 Written by The Financial Express 
 November 2, 2026 21:57 IST 
 Follow Us 
 NITI Aayog member Rajiv Gauba’s call for comprehensive reforms in urban governance, planning, and financing is timely and well-founded. India’s cities are increasingly struggling with overcrowding, rising air and noise pollution, inadequate infrastructure, and weak governance. By 2050, nearly 800 million people are expected to live in urban centres, up from around 500 million today, accounting for almost half the country’s population. This rapid urbanisation will place enormous demands on infrastructure, public services, and institutional capacity. The fiscal capacity of urban local bodies (ULBs) remains woefully inadequate. Municipal corporations’ revenue receipts amount to just 0.6% of GDP . Property tax is their largest revenue source, contributing over 15% of total receipts and more than 60% of their own tax revenue. However, the share of own resources in total ULB receipts has declined as key revenue sources were subsumed into the goods and services tax (GST) .
Despite limited revenues and heavy dependence on contingent transfers from higher government tiers, ULBs spend around 1.4% of GDP, with only marginal increases in recent years. This is considerably lower than the expenditure of urban bodies in comparable economies such as Brazil and South Africa. While ULBs in some states have witnessed a higher share of capital expenditure, this largely reflects the reallocation of scarce resources rather than an expansion of fiscal capacity. Moreover, more than half of ULBs’ revenue expenditure covers salaries, pensions, and administrative costs.
Without a substantial increase in investment in urban infrastructure and its effective maintenance, India’s expanding cities risk becoming increasingly dysfunctional and unliveable. The World Bank estimates that Indian cities will require `60 lakh crore in infrastructure investment between 2021 and 2036. The financing challenge is enormous, with capital investment requirements alone exceeding three times ULBs’ current revenue receipts. Although Finance Commission (FC) grants have increased, particularly by the 16th FC, strengthening municipal finances remains imperative. Rational user charges can mobilise additional revenue, but deepening the municipal bond market, currently less than 0.05% of GDP, is equally important to reduce dependence on central grants for infrastructure financing.
As of March 31, just 22 ULBs had raised Rs 4,540 crore through 31 municipal bond issuances, largely through private placements rather than public offerings. Municipal bonds account for less than 1% of India’s rupee bond market. This limited uptake persists despite incentives under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation 2.0, which offers up to Rs 13 crore for every Rs 100 crore raised by first-time municipal bond issuers. The Securities and Exchange Board of India has also advocated greater regulatory clarity and pooled financing mechanisms to facilitate bond issuance by smaller towns. However, financial incentives and regulatory interventions alone cannot strengthen urban governance without meaningful fiscal and functional autonomy, and resultant higher creditworthiness of ULBs. Despite the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments of 1993, local governments continue to face inadequate devolution of powers and resources. Correcting this deficit requires greater fiscal devolution, including a dedicated consolidated fund for local bodies and a mechanism to share a portion of GST proceeds directly with them. Equally important are participatory, bottom-up planning, community engagement, and rationalisation of local revenue sources. Performance-linked central grants must strengthen institutional capacity without undermining local autonomy or diminishing the role of states. Excessive conditionalities risk creating centralised decentralisation, defeating the very purpose of empowering local governments. Ultimately, sustainable urbanisation demands a shift from centrally-driven funding to empowered local institutions with predictable revenues, accountable governance, and the capacity to plan and deliver essential services.

docs.title: Chhattisgarh’s development push: Bastar peace, infrastructure and tourism to drive investment opportunities
docs.text: Chhattisgarh is looking to strengthen its position as an investment destination by combining infrastructure expansion, industrial development, tourism and employment generation, with the state government seeking to unlock the economic potential of resource-rich regions such as Bastar. Addressing the inauguration of the three-day Rajyotsav 2026 celebrations in Raipur on November 1, Union Minister Mansukh Mandaviya said Chhattisgarh's development would contribute to India's ambition of becoming a developed nation by 2047. He noted that the state's natural resources, cultural heritage, industrial potential and expanding infrastructure as key drivers of economic growth. Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai also outlined the government's development priorities, including improving connectivity in remote areas, expanding healthcare and education infrastructure, supporting farmers and women through welfare schemes, and attracting industrial investment. The emphasis on Bastar was particularly significant, with the state government seeking to move the region beyond the challenges posed by Naxalism and create opportunities in tourism, skill development, employment and industrial activity. ALSO READBJP holds ‘Loktantra Bachao’ rallies in Telangana, West Bengal; Amit Shah, Nitin Nabin lead Bastar's transition towards peace could open up economic opportunities Mandaviya said Bastar, which was previously associated largely with the challenge of Naxalism, was witnessing new opportunities in sports, tourism, culture and development. He said the region's natural resources and cultural heritage could support its economic transformation. Sai said Naxalism had historically prevented development facilities from reaching several parts of Bastar despite the region's forest wealth, mineral resources and natural attractions. He said improved security conditions were creating opportunities to expand roads, electricity, education, healthcare and communication infrastructure in remote villages. The state government is also looking to connect areas previously affected by Naxalism with the mainstream economy through skill development and employment opportunities for local youth. For the state's economy, improved connectivity and security could support greater economic activity in areas that have remained difficult to access. Tourism, local businesses and resource-based industries are among the sectors that could benefit from the expansion of infrastructure, although the pace of investment will depend on the development of supporting facilities. Tourism push could create opportunities for local businesses Tourism is emerging as another area of focus for Chhattisgarh, with the government seeking to promote destinations such as Chitrakote Waterfall, Sirpur, Rajim, the ancient caves of Ramgarh and Mainpat. State Culture Minister Rajesh Agrawal said these destinations had the potential to attract visitors from across India and abroad. Expanding tourism activity could create employment and income opportunities for local youth, women, artisans and small businesses. The state's tribal traditions and folk art forms, including Pandavani, Panthi and Dadariya, are also being positioned as part of its tourism and cultural economy. The government has undertaken initiatives to preserve traditional art forms and recognise artists, including instituting a state honour in memory of Pandavani exponent Teejan Bai. A stronger tourism ecosystem could support businesses in hospitality, transport, food services, handicrafts and local experiences. However, developing these opportunities would require investment in connectivity, accommodation, visitor facilities and tourism infrastructure. Industrial investment and infrastructure development remain key priorities Mandaviya said industrial investment, infrastructure expansion and employment generation were opening new possibilities for Chhattisgarh's development. He described the state's natural resources, workforce and cultural strengths as important assets in its effort to attract investment. The government is also seeking to expand basic infrastructure in remote regions, including roads, electricity and communication networks. These facilities are important for improving access to markets, supporting industrial activity and connecting businesses with wider supply chains. The emphasis on indigenous resources and local capabilities is expected to remain central to the state's development strategy. However, the government's broader investment ambitions will need to translate into actual projects, capital commitments and employment opportunities. ALSO READDelhi raises pollution curbs to ‘GRAP-II’ as air quality falls sharply Housing, farmer support and women's financial assistance The state government's welfare programmes also form part of its economic development strategy, with a focus on household incomes, rural demand and financial support for vulnerable sections. Sai said around 1,600 pucca houses were being completed every day under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana. The programme is aimed at improving housing access for low-income families while supporting construction-related economic activity. The chief minister said the state was procuring paddy from farmers at Rs 3,100 per quintal, up to 21 quintals per acre. The government has also paid pending paddy bonuses, he said. Under the Mahtari Vandan Yojana, more than 68 lakh women receive monthly financial assistance directly into their bank accounts. Sai said the scheme was helping strengthen women's financial independence and supporting household expenditure. The government has also restarted the Charan Paduka Yojana and is providing annual financial assistance of Rs 10,000 to landless agricultural labourers. These measures are intended to support rural and household incomes, potentially strengthening consumption demand across the state. docs.title: US Midterm Elections 2026: Date, voting time, key candidates and what to expect
docs.text: The 2026 US midterm elections will be held on Tuesday with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats up for election. Voters will also elect governors in 36 states, along with state legislators and local representatives. US President Donald Trump, though not on the ballot, continues to wage a war against the Democratic Party, calling its nominees "the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history" in his pre-midterm campaign. US Midterm Election 2026 LIVE: Follow latest news and updates here The elections will be the first nationwide electoral test of President Donald Trump's second term. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, but Democrats are hoping to win enough seats to take control of the House, the Senate or both. The campaign has been shaped by concerns over the cost of living, immigration enforcement, the US war with Iran and the economy. The results will determine how much legislative support Trump has during the final two years of his term and could influence both parties' strategies ahead of the 2028 presidential election. When are US midterm elections 2026? The US midterm elections will take place on November 3. Presidential elections are held every four years, while midterms take place halfway through a president's four-year term. Voters will elect: All 435 members of the House of Representatives. 35 of the 100 members of the Senate, including two special elections in Florida and Ohio. Governors in 36 states. State legislators and local representatives. Republicans will defend 22 Senate seats, while Democrats will defend 13, reported Indian Express. The party controlling Congress has significant influence over legislation, government spending, congressional investigations and oversight of the administration. A change in control of either chamber would therefore affect Trump's ability to advance his legislative agenda. What is at stake in the House and Senate? Republicans currently control both chambers, but the number of seats Democrats need to win differs between the House and Senate. docs.title: FE Exclusive | ‘Pulsar’s revival is gaining real momentum’: Bajaj Auto’s Rakesh Sharma
docs.text:
Sign In 
 CLOSE 
 For uninterrupted reading, switch to App
 READ IN APP 
 Written by Akbar Merchant 
 Updated: November 3, 2026 05:22 IST 
 Follow Us 
 Bajaj Auto is sharpening its focus on premium motorcycles, exports and electric mobility to drive growth in FY27. Rakesh Sharma, Joint Managing Director, Bajaj Auto, talks to Akbar Merchant about the Pulsar revival, upcoming motorcycle brands, record export performance and the company’s strategy to balance market share with profitability. Excerpts:
 Bajaj Auto remains outside India’s top three two-wheeler manufacturers. What are your priorities for regaining market share in FY27? 
India’s motorcycle business accounts for around 19% of our overall business, while our international operations across 108 countries contribute substantially. In India, our focus is on motorcycles of 125cc and above, alongside electric scooters .
The sub-125cc segment has declined from around 50% of the motorcycle market five years ago to approximately 45% now. We prioritise profitability, with operating profitability at 20.9%, which we believe is best-in-class globally. Our entry-level products are priced at a premium, and we accept some market-share loss to protect margins.
 Pulsar has faced market-share erosion. How is the refreshed portfolio performing? 
Pulsar sells around 100,000 units a month, but parts of the portfolio had reached the end of their product cycles. We began refreshing the range with the 250cc models, followed by the 160cc motorcycles, and are now seeing a reversal of market-share erosion in the 150cc-plus segment.
The NS range is growing at roughly twice the market rate, while the classic range has also been upgraded. The contribution of new products to our 250cc-and-above portfolio increased from 7% in August to 26% in September and 34% during the first 16 days of the festive period. We expect the entire 125cc-to-400cc Pulsar portfolio to be refreshed by January 1.
 What are your plans for the two new motorcycle brands in FY27? 
One brand will target an emerging sub-segment with significant potential, identified through an understanding of India’s demographics and international markets. The second will strengthen our presence in the 125cc-to-150cc space. Both will complement Pulsar and address distinct market opportunities.
 Is adventure motorcycling another growth opportunity? 
Adventure and soft-adventure motorcycles account for around 7% of India’s market but are growing four times faster than the overall market. Through KTM adventure motorcycles and Triumph scramblers, we are leaders in this segment. KTM’s Dakar heritage, engineering and brand strength give us strong credentials.
 Will Bajaj introduce another electric two-wheeler brand beyond Chetak? 
Electric scooters account for around 25% of the scooter market, and penetration could reach 50% in three to five years. Chetak has five variants catering to different customer groups. We are open to a second brand if a distinct customer segment and usage pattern emerge, but we are not actively evaluating one at present.
We are also examining electric motorcycles for India and international markets. However, battery space and range remain challenges. On dealer margins, we see no immediate need for restructuring, as higher EV prices can support reasonable earnings even at similar percentage margins.
 How have exports performed in H1 FY27, and which markets are driving growth? 
Exports crossed 1.5 million units in H1, growing over 40% year-on-year and marking record performances for both the first half and the quarter.
Africa has been the biggest driver. While the industry grew around 35%, we grew 83%. Nigeria’s market has recovered to approximately 30,000-35,000 units a month from a low of 15,000, and our market share stands at 55-60%. Our share exceeds 50% in Kenya and is around 80% in Uganda. Ethiopia remains constrained by foreign-exchange restrictions.
Latin America is the second major growth driver. The industry grew around 12%, while we grew 44%, with Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, Central America, Argentina and Peru among our key markets. Sportier Pulsar and Dominar models also deliver a better product mix and higher margins.
In Asia, the industry declined around 7%, but our volumes grew 5%. In the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), industry volumes fell around 29%, while ours declined 24%, reflecting the impact of the war. Africa contributes around 50% of our international business, Latin America 35%, and Asia and MENA the remaining 15%.
 How has Bajaj’s share of India’s motorcycle and three-wheeler exports changed? 
Our share of motorcycle exports from India rose from 44% last year to 48% in H1 FY27, meaning nearly one in every two motorcycles exported from India carries the Bajaj brand. Our share of three-wheeler exports increased from 60% to 63%.
 What are your key growth priorities going forward? 
Our priorities are motorcycles in the 125cc-plus segment, international business, electric two-wheelers and electric three-wheelers. We see opportunities to gain share in India’s 150cc-plus segment, expand our presence in Africa and Latin America, build on our leadership in electric three-wheelers and strengthen our electric scooter business.

docs.text:
Despite the stock remaining under severe selling pressure and losing 38% of its value in 2026 so far to trade at around ₹ 1,036 apiece, the brokerage remains confident about its long-term growth prospects. It believes the company is positioned for renewed growth acceleration, citing expectations of a recovery in pre-sales, supported by the enhanced gross development value (GDV) of Niyaara Tower C and a stronger launch pipeline. Anand Rathi said that the company is transitioning from a Worli-led growth story to a diversified, capital-efficient real estate platform, with an expanding multi-city portfolio and commercial annuity assets. It highlighted that Worli residential portfolio accounts for approximately ₹ 243 billion (50%) of the company's approximately ₹ 483 billion upcoming launch pipeline, making it the key contributor to near-term launch visibility, with the planned Tower C launch expected to drive the next phase of Worli-led growth. Anand Rathi said that following a sharp scale-up in pre-sales on the back of strong business development (BD) during FY23-25, a moderation in BD additions and deferment of the Niyaara Tower C launch to FY28 are likely to weigh on FY27 pre-sales. However, the brokerage believes the deferment is value-accretive, with the redesign and amalgamation of adjoining land parcels adding approximately ₹ 19 billion to the overall Worli gross development value (GDV). With approximately ₹ 60 billion of BD additions year-to-date (YTD), a further ₹ 600 billion opportunity pipeline and a stronger launch pipeline from FY28, Anand Rathi expects pre-sales to regain momentum, supporting management's target of ₹ 150 billion by FY29. The brokerage added that improving collections, divestment proceeds, and selective joint development agreement (JDA)/joint venture (JV) partnerships offer financial flexibility to replenish the pipeline while containing capital intensity. Anand Rathi said ABREL has established a multi-city development platform through 14 BD transactions across FY23-27 YTD. With approximately ₹ 483 billion of planned launches and a further ₹ 600 billion BD opportunity pipeline, timely conversion and execution will be critical to sustain growth and drive recovery in pre-sales from FY28E.
